title: How to pay for software with a Russian card via Prodamus — safe, with a receipt
summary:
When you buy software online from a small independent author, two questions always come up: will my card payment go through and is it safe to enter my card details. Here are honest answers in plain words. Payments on my site are handled by Prodamus — a well-known Russian payment provider — so this guide is most useful if you pay with a Russian card.

What Prodamus is

Prodamus is a well-known Russian payment service. In simple terms, it is a secure “checkout” that processes the payment. When you press the pay button on the site, you are redirected to a Prodamus page where you enter your card details. The money goes directly through the payment system, and as the seller I only see the fact that the payment was made — not your card.

Is it safe to enter card details

Yes. This is the main question, and the answer is simple:

  • You enter card details on the payment system's side, not on my website.

  • The website never sees or stores your card number, expiry date, or the code on the back.

  • The connection is encrypted — the payment page runs over a secure protocol (the padlock icon in your browser).

So your payment data never reaches me or the site's hosting — it stays inside the secure environment of the bank and the payment system.

Which cards you can use

Prodamus accepts Russian cards:

  • Mir cards from any bank.

  • Visa and Mastercard issued by Russian banks.

  • SBP (Fast Payments System) by QR code, when that option is shown on the payment page.

If you pay with a foreign card (issued outside Russia), the site has a separate method for that — via the lava.top service.

Will you get a receipt

Yes. Prodamus issues a fiscal receipt and sends it to you — to the email or phone you provide at checkout. It is a real cash receipt, not just a “thank you for your purchase” note. So the purchase is documented officially.

How the payment works, step by step

  • Pick a program on the site and press the pay button.

  • A Prodamus page opens with the amount and the program name.

  • Enter your card details and confirm the payment (your bank may send an SMS code).

  • You receive a receipt by email and access to the full version of the program.

What happens after payment

After a successful payment you get the full version of the program — without the demo limits. Activation is tied to your computer, so there are no long serial numbers to type in by hand.

If something goes wrong

You can always get a refund under the refund rules. If a payment “hangs” or does not go through, write to me at info@evgeniymamonov.com and we will sort it out.

Which programs this works for

Prodamus can be used to pay for any of my Windows programs:

  • Ekrannik — one-click screen recording with sound.

  • Kadrik — splits a video into sharp frames (photos).

  • Diktik — turns speech into text.

Each program has a free demo — try it on your own tasks first, and pay only when you decide to use the full version.

In short

Paying via Prodamus from Russia is safe: a Mir, Visa, or Mastercard card from a Russian bank will work, the site never sees your card details, and after payment you get a real receipt. All that is left is to pick a program and try the demo.

title: Build a CLI Task Manager in Python with argparse and Rich
summary:
A command line interface, or CLI, is a program we control by typing commands in a terminal instead of clicking buttons in a window. Python ships with argparse, a module that parses those commands and prints help text for us. We build a task manager CLI with argparse and Rich tables, and we run each command to prove it works.

Key takeaways

  • argparse turns a few declarations into a full command parser, with help text, type checks and error messages included.
  • Subparsers give a tool git style commands, so tasks add, tasks list, tasks done and tasks delete each take their own arguments.
  • Rich draws readable tables in the terminal from a few lines of code, and it colours priorities and statuses without manual escape codes.
  • A JSON file is enough storage for a personal CLI tool, and it keeps the data human readable.
  • Running the tool end to end caught a real bug in our delete command, which we fixed before publishing.

What we build

We build tasks.py, a task manager that lives in the terminal. It stores tasks in a tasks.json file next to the script, and it offers four commands. add creates a task with a title and a priority of low, medium or high. list shows tasks in a Rich table, with an optional --status filter. done marks a task complete by its ID, and delete removes one. The whole tool is one file of about 150 lines, it needs no server and no database, and it runs on any machine with Python 3.12 or newer.

What do we need before we start?

We need Python 3.12 or newer and the Rich library. We ran this tutorial with Python 3.12.3 and Rich 15.0.0, installed with pip install rich inside a virtual environment. A virtual environment keeps Rich separate from the system Python, so the tutorial never touches packages other projects rely on. Rich is the only dependency. argparse needs no install because it ships with Python, and the JSON storage uses the standard library too. We keep the code in a folder called cli-task-manager so the script and its data file sit together.

Step 1: Set up the project and install Rich

We create the folder and install Rich in our virtual environment. Rich renders tables, colours and progress bars in the terminal, and it is the library behind the Textual terminal framework, according to the Rich documentation.

mkdir cli-task-manager
cd cli-task-manager
pip install rich

Our install pulled in Rich 15.0.0 with its small dependencies, markdown-it-py and Pygments. We check the install with a one-liner that prints both versions, because every version number in this tutorial is one we measured, not one we guessed.

python -c "import sys; from importlib.metadata import version; print('Python', sys.version.split()[0]); print('rich', version('rich'))"

Python 3.12.3
rich 15.0.0

Step 2: How do subcommands work in argparse?

Subcommands are the pattern behind tools like git and docker, where the first word after the program name picks the action. argparse models this with add_subparsers(). We create one parser for the whole tool, then one subparser per command, and we attach a handler function to each subparser with set_defaults(func=...). After parsing, we call the attached function with the parsed arguments. Each subparser also gets its own help text, so tasks add --help explains only the add command.

One detail worth knowing: add_subparsers() takes required=True, which makes argparse print a clear error when we run tasks with no command at all instead of silently doing nothing. Without it, a bare run exits quietly and the user has no idea what went wrong.

def build_parser():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        prog="tasks",
        description="A small task manager for the terminal.",
    )
    sub = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)

    p_add = sub.add_parser("add", help="Add a new task")
    p_add.add_argument("title", help="What needs doing")
    p_add.add_argument("--priority", choices=("low", "medium", "high"),
                       default="medium", help="Task priority (default: medium)")
    p_add.set_defaults(func=cmd_add)

    p_list = sub.add_parser("list", help="List tasks")
    p_list.add_argument("--status", choices=("all", "todo", "done"),
                        default="all", help="Which tasks to show (default: all)")
    p_list.set_defaults(func=cmd_list)

    p_done = sub.add_parser("done", help="Mark a task as done")
    p_done.add_argument("task_id", type=int, help="ID of the task")
    p_done.set_defaults(func=cmd_done)

    p_delete = sub.add_parser("delete", help="Delete a task")
    p_delete.add_argument("task_id", type=int, help="ID of the task")
    p_delete.set_defaults(func=cmd_delete)

    return parser

def main():
    parser = build_parser()
    args = parser.parse_args()
    args.func(args)

Notice the two kinds of arguments. title and task_id are positional, so they are required and given without a flag. --priority and --status are optional flags with choices, which means argparse rejects anything outside the list before our code ever runs. type=int on task_id converts the text to a number and rejects done abc with a clear error.

Step 3: Store tasks in a JSON file

We keep storage simple. Each task is a dictionary with an ID, a title, a priority and a done flag, and the whole list lives in tasks.json. Two tiny functions handle the file, and a third hands out the next ID.

import argparse
import json
from pathlib import Path

from rich.console import Console
from rich.table import Table

DATA_FILE = Path(__file__).with_name("tasks.json")
console = Console()

PRIORITIES = ("low", "medium", "high")

def load_tasks():
    if not DATA_FILE.exists():
        return []
    return json.loads(DATA_FILE.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

def save_tasks(tasks):
    DATA_FILE.write_text(json.dumps(tasks, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")

def next_id(tasks):
    return max((task["id"] for task in tasks), default=0) + 1

We place the data file next to the script with Path(file).with_name("tasks.json") instead of a relative path, so the tool works no matter which folder we run it from. load_tasks returns an empty list when the file does not exist yet, which is the correct behaviour for a first run. JSON keeps the data readable in any text editor, and that matters when we debug the tool later.

Step 4: Add the add and list commands

The add command loads the tasks, appends a new dictionary and saves the list. The list command filters by status, then builds a Rich table with one row per task. Rich colours the priority and the status, so a quick scan shows what is urgent and what is finished.

def cmd_add(args):
    tasks = load_tasks()
    task = {
        "id": next_id(tasks),
        "title": args.title,
        "priority": args.priority,
        "done": False,
    }
    tasks.append(task)
    save_tasks(tasks)
    console.print(f"[green]Added task #{task['id']}:[/green] {task['title']} "
                  f"({task['priority']} priority)")

def cmd_list(args):
    tasks = load_tasks()
    if args.status == "done":
        tasks = [t for t in tasks if t["done"]]
    elif args.status == "todo":
        tasks = [t for t in tasks if not t["done"]]

    if not tasks:
        console.print("[yellow]No tasks found. Add one with:[/yellow] "
                      "python tasks.py add \"Buy milk\"")
        return

    table = Table(title="Tasks")
    table.add_column("ID", justify="right", style="cyan")
    table.add_column("Title", style="white")
    table.add_column("Priority", justify="center")
    table.add_column("Status", justify="center")
    for task in tasks:
        status = "[green]done[/green]" if task["done"] else "[yellow]todo[/yellow]"
        colour = {"high": "red", "medium": "yellow", "low": "dim"}.get(task["priority"], "white")
        table.add_row(str(task["id"]), task["title"],
                      f"[{colour}]{task['priority']}[/{colour}]", status)
    console.print(table)

The square brackets in the strings are Rich markup, not plain text. [green]...[/green] colours the text inside, and console.print interprets it. When output is piped to a file, Rich strips the colours automatically, so the same code prints clean text in logs.

Step 5: Add done and delete, and fix a real bug

The done command finds a task by ID, flips its flag and saves. The delete command builds a new list without the task and saves that list instead. When we first ran the tool end to end, delete printed its success message but the task stayed in the file. The bug was one wrong variable name: the function filtered the list into kept and then saved the original tasks list. We fixed it by saving kept, and the retest below proves the fix.

def cmd_done(args):
    tasks = load_tasks()
    for task in tasks:
        if task["id"] == args.task_id:
            if task["done"]:
                console.print(f"[yellow]Task #{args.task_id} is already done.[/yellow]")
                return
            task["done"] = True
            save_tasks(tasks)
            console.print(f"[green]Done:[/green] {task['title']}")
            return
    console.print(f"[red]No task with ID {args.task_id}.[/red]")

def cmd_delete(args):
    tasks = load_tasks()
    kept = [t for t in tasks if t["id"] != args.task_id]
    if len(kept) == len(tasks):
        console.print(f"[red]No task with ID {args.task_id}.[/red]")
        return
    save_tasks(kept)
    console.print(f"[green]Deleted task #{args.task_id}.[/green]")

Both commands handle a missing ID with a plain message instead of crashing. That is a small choice with a large effect on how the tool feels: a tool that says "No task with ID 99" is one we trust, and a tool that dumps a traceback is one we stop using.

Step 6: Run the whole tool end to end

We delete the data file and run a full session: add three tasks, complete one, delete one, and list what is left. This is the real output from our run.

python tasks.py add "Write the weekly report" --priority high
python tasks.py add "Buy printer paper"
python tasks.py add "Review pull request 42" --priority low
python tasks.py done 2
python tasks.py delete 3

Added task #1: Write the weekly report (high priority)
Added task #2: Buy printer paper (medium priority)
Added task #3: Review pull request 42 (low priority)
Done: Buy printer paper
Deleted task #3.

The final list shows only the two tasks that remain, and the JSON file on disk agrees with it. The file holds two entries, task 1 still open and task 2 marked done, which is exactly the state the commands produced.

python tasks.py list

Tasks
┏━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━┓
┃ ID ┃ Title                   ┃ Priority ┃ Status ┃
┡━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━┩
│  1 │ Write the weekly report │   high   │  todo  │
│  2 │ Buy printer paper       │  medium  │  done  │
└────┴─────────────────────────┴──────────┴────────┘

Two checks confirm the validation works. Filtering to done tasks shows only task 2, and an invalid priority is rejected by argparse before our code runs, with exit code 2.

python tasks.py list --status done
python tasks.py add "x" --priority urgent

Tasks
┏━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━┓

│  2 │ Buy printer paper │  medium  │  done  │
└────┴───────────────────┴──────────┴────────┘
tasks add: error: argument --priority: invalid choice: 'urgent' (choose from 'low', 'medium', 'high')

The help text is free. python tasks.py --help lists all four commands, and python tasks.py add --help explains only the add command, because argparse generates both from the declarations we wrote in step 2.

usage: tasks [-h] {add,list,done,delete} ...

A small task manager for the terminal.

positional arguments:
  {add,list,done,delete}
    add                 Add a new task
    list                List tasks
    done                Mark a task as done
    delete              Delete a task

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit

What to try next

First, add due dates with a --due flag and sort the table by date, which teaches custom type functions in argparse. Second, add an edit subcommand that changes a task title by ID, which reuses the same load, change and save pattern as done. Third, package the tool with a pyproject.toml entry point so tasks runs from anywhere without typing python tasks.py first.

        console.print(f"[red]No task with ID {args.task_id}.[/red]")
        return
    save_tasks(kept)
    console.print(f"[green]Deleted task #{args.task_id}.[/green]")

Both commands handle a missing ID with a plain message instead of crashing. That is a small choice with a large effect on how the tool feels: a tool that says "No task with ID 99" is one we trust, and a tool that dumps a traceback is one we stop using.

Step 6: Run the whole tool end to end

We delete the data file and run a full session: add three tasks, complete one, delete one, and list what is left. This is the real output from our run.

python tasks.py add "Write the weekly report" --priority high
python tasks.py add "Buy printer paper"
python tasks.py add "Review pull request 42" --priority low
python tasks.py done 2
python tasks.py delete 3

Added task #2: Buy printer paper (medium priority)
Added task #3: Review pull request 42 (low priority)
Done: Buy printer paper
Deleted task #3.

The final list shows only the two tasks that remain, and the JSON file on disk agrees with it. The file holds two entries, task 1 still open and task 2 marked done, which is exactly the state the commands produced.

python tasks.py list

The help text is free. python tasks.py --help lists all four commands, and python tasks.py add --help explains only the add command, because argparse generates both from the declarations we wrote in step 2.

What to try next

First, add due dates with a --due flag and sort the table by date, which teaches custom type functions in argparse. Second, add an edit subcommand that changes a task title by ID, which reuses the same load, change and save pattern as done. Third, package the tool with a pyproject.toml entry point so tasks runs from anywhere without typing python tasks.py first.

title: Does My Bama Bound AI Clip Have a Glitch Frame? Finding Cuts, Flashes, Freezes and Skipped Frames in Python
summary:
Checked November 13, 2026 (15:00 CST, UTC+8). I build bamabound.app, which turns one photo of one person into a vertical clip of them holding a red I'M BAMA BOUND banner. Every clip in this post is a synthetic stand-in (a red "TEST BANNER" box swaying over a grainy green field, 720x1280, 30 fps, 8 s), not a real person and not a real generated clip.

People ask some version of this a lot: "There's a weird blink in the middle of my Bama Bound video. Is that a glitch, or did my editor do it?"

An AI clip is about eight seconds long (FAQ). At normal speed, a single odd frame is easy to feel and hard to find. You scrub, it's gone, you scrub back, you can't land on it. What you want is a list: frame 90, white flash, one frame long. Then you can look at exactly that frame, cut it, or send it to whoever made the clip.

This post builds that list with about 150 lines of Python, numpy and ffmpeg. I test it on five planted defects plus two clips that should come back clean, and compare it with ffmpeg's built-in scdet filter, which turned out to catch only two of the four defect types.

Four kinds of "jump", and what they look like in numbers

The whole method rests on one number per frame: how different is this frame from the one before it? Decode the clip very small (36 px wide, so film grain averages out), take the mean absolute RGB difference with the previous frame, and you get a 0-255 value. On my grainy test clip it sits around 1.1 for normal motion.

Defect What you see Shape of the difference curve
Hard cut the picture switches to a different shot one huge spike, and the picture stays different
Flash frame 1-3 frames of white/black/garbage a spike in, a spike out, and the frames either side match each other
Freeze motion stops, then resumes a run of near-zero differences
Skipped frames the banner "teleports" a little one moderate spike, a few times the usual motion

The skip is the sneaky one. Dropping 15 frames of a slowly swaying banner gave a difference of about 4 against a typical 1.1. That's visible to the eye, but nowhere near what a scene-cut detector is tuned for.

Judge each clip by its own motion

A fixed threshold doesn't work. A clip with lots of motion has big frame-to-frame differences everywhere. A calm one has tiny ones. So the script compares each difference with a rolling median over a one-second window around it. A spike counts when it is more than 4x that local median and above an absolute floor of 6. A skip counts at 2.5x local motion, 1.5x the clip's overall median and at least 1.0. A freeze is a run of frames under a tenth of the typical motion that lasts at least 0.3 s.

That 0.3 s number came from a false alarm, which I'll get to below.

The script 

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""jumpcheck.py - find sudden jumps in a short clip: hard cuts, flash frames,
freezes and skipped frames.

It decodes the clip at a small size (default 36 px wide), measures how much each
frame differs from the one before it (mean absolute RGB difference, 0-255),
and compares every difference with the clip's own typical motion (a rolling
median), so a slow clip and a busy clip are judged on their own terms.

    python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4            # human-readable report
    python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4 --json     # machine-readable
    python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4 --csv d.csv  # per-frame differences

Exit code 0 = nothing found (keyframe pulses are listed but not counted),
1 = at least one cut/flash/freeze/skip, 2 = could not read clip.
Needs ffmpeg/ffprobe on PATH and numpy.
"""
import argparse, json, subprocess, sys
import numpy as np


def probe(path):
    out = subprocess.run(
        ["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-select_streams", "v:0", "-show_entries",
         "stream=width,height,avg_frame_rate", "-of", "json", path],
        capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout
    s = json.loads(out)["streams"][0]
    num, den = s["avg_frame_rate"].split("/")
    return int(s["width"]), int(s["height"]), float(num) / float(den)


def frames(path, w, h):
    cmd = ["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", path, "-an", "-vf",
           f"scale={w}:{h}:flags=area", "-pix_fmt", "rgb24", "-f", "rawvideo", "-"]
    raw = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    n = len(raw) // (w * h * 3)
    return np.frombuffer(raw[: n * w * h * 3], np.uint8).reshape(n, h, w, 3).astype(np.int16)


def keyframes(path):
    """Indices of I-frames. Low-bitrate encodes 'pulse' on every keyframe,
    which looks like a small skip but is just the encoder refreshing detail."""
    out = subprocess.run(
        ["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-select_streams", "v:0", "-show_entries",
         "frame=pict_type", "-of", "csv=p=0", path],
        capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout.split()
    return {i for i, t in enumerate(out) if t.strip(",") == "I"}


def diff(a, b):
    return float(np.abs(a - b).mean())


def analyse(path, small_w=36, spike=4.0, floor=6.0, freeze_ratio=0.1, min_freeze_s=0.3):
    W, H, fps = probe(path)
    small_h = max(2, round(small_w * H / W / 2) * 2)
    f = frames(path, small_w, small_h)
    n = len(f)
    kf = keyframes(path)
    min_freeze = max(2, int(round(min_freeze_s * fps)))
    d = np.zeros(n)
    for i in range(1, n):
        d[i] = diff(f[i], f[i - 1])
    # typical motion around each frame: median of a 1-second window, excluding frame 0
    win = max(5, int(round(fps)))
    base = np.zeros(n)
    for i in range(1, n):
        lo, hi = max(1, i - win), min(n, i + win + 1)
        base[i] = np.median(d[lo:hi])
    typical = float(np.median(d[1:])) if n > 1 else 0.0
    events, i = [], 1
    is_spike = lambda k: d[k] > max(spike * base[k], floor)
    while i < n:
        if is_spike(i):
            # flash: spike in, spike out within 3 frames, and the frames either side match
            back = None
            for k in range(1, 4):
                j = i + k
                if j < n and is_spike(j) and diff(f[i - 1], f[j]) < max(spike * base[i], floor) / 2:
                    back = j
                    break
            if back:
                events.append({"type": "flash", "frame": i, "frames": back - i,
                               "time": round(i / fps, 3), "diff": round(float(d[i]), 2)})
                i = back + 1
                continue
            # does the picture stay changed? compare a frame before with a frame after
            after = min(n - 1, i + 2)
            kind = "cut" if diff(f[i - 1], f[after]) > max(spike * base[i], floor) else "jump"
            events.append({"type": kind, "frame": i, "time": round(i / fps, 3),
                           "diff": round(float(d[i]), 2), "typical": round(float(base[i]), 2)})
        elif d[i] < freeze_ratio * max(typical, 1e-6):
            j = i
            while j < n and d[j] < freeze_ratio * max(typical, 1e-6):
                j += 1
            if j - i + 1 >= min_freeze:
                events.append({"type": "freeze", "frame": i - 1, "frames": j - i + 1,
                               "time": round((i - 1) / fps, 3),
                               "seconds": round((j - i + 1) / fps, 3)})
            i = j
            continue
        elif d[i] > max(2.5 * base[i], 1.5 * typical) and d[i] > 1.0:
            events.append({"type": "keyframe" if i in kf else "skip", "frame": i, "time": round(i / fps, 3),
                           "diff": round(float(d[i]), 2), "typical": round(float(base[i]), 2)})
        i += 1
    return {"file": path, "frames": n, "fps": round(fps, 3), "size": f"{W}x{H}",
            "typical_diff": round(typical, 3), "max_diff": round(float(d.max()), 2),
            "events": events}, d


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.split("\n")[0])
    ap.add_argument("clip")
    ap.add_argument("--json", action="store_true")
    ap.add_argument("--csv")
    ap.add_argument("--width", type=int, default=36, help="analysis width in px (smaller = less grain)")
    ap.add_argument("--min-freeze", type=float, default=0.3, help="seconds of no change that count as a freeze")
    ap.add_argument("--spike", type=float, default=4.0, help="x typical motion that counts as a spike")
    a = ap.parse_args()
    try:
        rep, d = analyse(a.clip, small_w=a.width, spike=a.spike, min_freeze_s=a.min_freeze)
    except (subprocess.CalledProcessError, KeyError, IndexError, ValueError) as e:
        print(f"could not read {a.clip}: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    if a.csv:
        with open(a.csv, "w") as fh:
            fh.write("frame,time,diff\n")
            for i, v in enumerate(d):
                fh.write(f"{i},{i / rep['fps']:.3f},{v:.3f}\n")
    if a.json:
        print(json.dumps(rep, indent=2))
    else:
        print(f"{rep['file']}: {rep['frames']} frames @ {rep['fps']} fps, {rep['size']}, "
              f"typical frame-to-frame diff {rep['typical_diff']}, max {rep['max_diff']}")
        if not rep["events"]:
            print("  no cuts, flashes, freezes or skips found")
        for e in rep["events"]:
            extra = {k: v for k, v in e.items() if k not in ("type", "frame", "time")}
            print(f"  {e['type']:6} at {e['time']:6.3f}s (frame {e['frame']})  {extra}")
    real = [e for e in rep["events"] if e["type"] != "keyframe"]
    if any(e["type"] == "keyframe" for e in rep["events"]):
        print("  (keyframe = small pulse on an I-frame, usually encoder refresh; not counted)")
    return 1 if real else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

Run it:

python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4          # report, exit 1 if anything found
python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4 --json   # for CI or a batch script
python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4 --csv diffs.csv   # plot the curve yourself

Planting defects to test it

You can't trust a detector you've only run on clean clips. make_glitch.sh takes any clip and plants one known defect at a known frame:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Make a test copy of a clip with one known defect, to check a jump detector.
#   ./make_glitch.sh in.mp4 cut|flash|freeze|drop|lowbitrate N out.mp4
#   cut        N ignored: from 4 s on, the picture is flipped and hue-rotated (a "different shot")
#   flash      N white frames starting at frame 90
#   freeze     frame 150 held for N frames (same total length)
#   drop       N frames removed starting at frame 120 (clip gets shorter, motion jumps)
#   lowbitrate N ignored: CRF 38 with a keyframe every 30 frames (encoder pulse, not a defect)
set -euo pipefail
in=$1; kind=$2; n=$3; out=$4
enc=(-c:v libx264 -preset veryfast -crf 20 -pix_fmt yuv420p)
case $kind in
  cut) ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$in" -filter_complex \
        "[0:v]split[a][b];[a]trim=0:4,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS[a2];[b]trim=4,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS,vflip,hue=h=120[b2];[a2][b2]concat=n=2:v=1:a=0,fps=30[v]" \
        -map "[v]" -map 0:a? "${enc[@]}" -c:a copy "$out" ;;
  flash) ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$in" -vf "drawbox=0:0:iw:ih:color=white:t=fill:enable='between(n,90,$((90+n-1)))'" \
        "${enc[@]}" -c:a copy "$out" ;;
  freeze) ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$in" -filter_complex "[0:v]split[a][b];[a][b]freezeframes=first=150:last=$((150+n-1)):replace=150[v]" \
        -map "[v]" -map 0:a? "${enc[@]}" -c:a copy "$out" ;;
  drop) ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$in" -vf "select='not(between(n,120,$((120+n-1))))',setpts=N/30/TB" -an -r 30 "${enc[@]}" "$out" ;;
  lowbitrate) ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$in" -c:v libx264 -preset veryfast -crf 38 -g 30 -pix_fmt yuv420p -c:a copy "$out" ;;
  *) echo "unknown kind $kind" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac
echo "wrote $out ($kind $n)"

The base clip comes from a small synthetic generator (make_field_test_clip.sh: gradient sky, noisy field, red box with white text swaying on a sine, beeps over a hum). It's in the same folder as the scripts.

Results

Same base clip, one defect at a time:

Test clip jumpcheck.py found Exit
clean clip, grain 18 nothing (typical diff 1.07, max 1.54) 0
hard cut at 4.0 s cut at frame 120, diff 102.3 vs local 1.12 1
1 white frame at 3.0 s flash at frame 90, 1 frame 1
2 white frames at 3.0 s flash at frame 90, 2 frames 1
frame 150 held 15 frames freeze at 5.0 s, 0.5 s 1
15 frames dropped at 4.0 s skip at frame 120, diff 4.06 vs 1.11 1
clean clip, no grain nothing (typical 0.245) 0
clean clip scaled to 480x854 nothing 0
clean clip re-encoded CRF 38, keyframe every 30 7 keyframe pulses listed, not counted 0
file that doesn't exist error message 2

For comparison: ffmpeg's scdet

ffmpeg ships a scene-change filter, so the obvious question is why not just use it:

ffmpeg -i clip.mp4 -vf "scdet=threshold=10,metadata=print:file=scd.txt" -f null -

On the same planted clips at threshold=10:

Defect Highest lavfi.scd.score Flagged?
clean 0.17 no
hard cut 24.5 (frame 120) yes
1 white frame 36.8 (frame 90) yes, but only the entry. The exit frame scored low, so it looks just like a cut
15-frame freeze 2.4 no
15 dropped frames 0.9 no

That isn't a bug. scdet is built to find scene changes, and its score is roughly "how much did the frame difference jump compared with the previous difference". The return from a flash is a big difference right after another big difference, so it scores low. Freezes and small skips aren't scene changes at all. If all you need is real cuts, scdet is fine. To tell a flash from a cut, or catch the quieter defects, you need the raw curve.

Two false alarms that shaped the defaults

1. Low-bitrate keyframe "pulses." I re-encoded the clean clip at CRF 38 with a keyframe every 30 frames. The first version of the script reported seven "skips" at frames 29, 58, 87 and so on, exactly 29 frames apart. ffprobe -show_entries frame=pict_type showed an I-frame at every one of them. At low bitrate, every keyframe refreshes detail the P-frames had smeared away, and that registers as a small jump. The script now asks ffprobe for I-frame positions, labels those events keyframe and leaves them out of the exit code.

The cost of that choice is that a real skip landing on a keyframe gets hidden. This happened once in the dataset grid I mention below. Before I made the test clip deterministic, a 10-frame drop got labelled keyframe because x264 had put an I-frame right at the jump. If you have a clip that already feels wrong, also read the keyframe lines.

2. Slow motion looks like a freeze. With grain turned off, the test banner moves less than a pixel per frame at the slow ends of its sway. After encoding, some frames come out identical. The first version flagged eight "freezes" of 3-7 frames (0.1-0.23 s) in a perfectly fine clip. Raising the minimum to 0.3 s removed all of them and still caught the planted 15-frame freeze. A 0.1 s pause in an AI clip is rarely what people mean by "it froze".

Where it stops working

  • Tiny skips are invisible. On the grainy clip, dropping 1, 2 or 5 frames wasn't detected. The motion jump is smaller than the grain. On the grain-free clip, 5 dropped frames were caught (diff 1.59 vs typical 0.244) but 1-2 weren't. Freezes of 3 and 6 frames were not reported (by design, under 0.3 s); 9 and 15 were. A full grid of these cases is in the dataset linked at the end.
  • A cut to a similar-looking shot can slip through. My cut fixture flips the picture and rotates the hue, so it's an obvious change. A cut between two nearly identical framings won't produce a big spike.
  • The freeze after-effect. When a freeze ends, the motion catches up in one frame. On the grain-free clip that catch-up was also reported as a skip. It isn't a second defect, just the other end of the same freeze.
  • Thresholds were tuned on synthetic clips. Real footage with camera shake will need --spike raised.

What to do with the list

event_model_payload.headline: Does My Bama Bound AI Clip Have a Glitch Frame? Finding Cuts, Flashes, Freezes and Skipped Frames in Python
event_model_payload.summary:
Checked November 13, 2026 (15:00 CST, UTC+8). I build bamabound.app, which turns one photo of one person into a vertical clip of them holding a red I'M BAMA BOUND banner. Every clip in this post is a synthetic stand-in (a red "TEST BANNER" box swaying over a grainy green field, 720x1280, 30 fps, 8 s), not a real person and not a real generated clip.

People ask some version of this a lot: "There's a weird blink in the middle of my Bama Bound video. Is that a glitch, or did my editor do it?"

An AI clip is about eight seconds long (FAQ). At normal speed, a single odd frame is easy to feel and hard to find. You scrub, it's gone, you scrub back, you can't land on it. What you want is a list: frame 90, white flash, one frame long. Then you can look at exactly that frame, cut it, or send it to whoever made the clip.

This post builds that list with about 150 lines of Python, numpy and ffmpeg. I test it on five planted defects plus two clips that should come back clean, and compare it with ffmpeg's built-in scdet filter, which turned out to catch only two of the four defect types.

Four kinds of "jump", and what they look like in numbers

The whole method rests on one number per frame: how different is this frame from the one before it? Decode the clip very small (36 px wide, so film grain averages out), take the mean absolute RGB difference with the previous frame, and you get a 0-255 value. On my grainy test clip it sits around 1.1 for normal motion.

Defect What you see Shape of the difference curve
Hard cut the picture switches to a different shot one huge spike, and the picture stays different
Flash frame 1-3 frames of white/black/garbage a spike in, a spike out, and the frames either side match each other
Freeze motion stops, then resumes a run of near-zero differences
Skipped frames the banner "teleports" a little one moderate spike, a few times the usual motion

The skip is the sneaky one. Dropping 15 frames of a slowly swaying banner gave a difference of about 4 against a typical 1.1. That's visible to the eye, but nowhere near what a scene-cut detector is tuned for.

Judge each clip by its own motion

A fixed threshold doesn't work. A clip with lots of motion has big frame-to-frame differences everywhere. A calm one has tiny ones. So the script compares each difference with a rolling median over a one-second window around it. A spike counts when it is more than 4x that local median and above an absolute floor of 6. A skip counts at 2.5x local motion, 1.5x the clip's overall median and at least 1.0. A freeze is a run of frames under a tenth of the typical motion that lasts at least 0.3 s.

That 0.3 s number came from a false alarm, which I'll get to below.

The script 

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""jumpcheck.py - find sudden jumps in a short clip: hard cuts, flash frames,
freezes and skipped frames.

It decodes the clip at a small size (default 36 px wide), measures how much each
frame differs from the one before it (mean absolute RGB difference, 0-255),
and compares every difference with the clip's own typical motion (a rolling
median), so a slow clip and a busy clip are judged on their own terms.

    python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4            # human-readable report
    python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4 --json     # machine-readable
    python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4 --csv d.csv  # per-frame differences

Exit code 0 = nothing found (keyframe pulses are listed but not counted),
1 = at least one cut/flash/freeze/skip, 2 = could not read clip.
Needs ffmpeg/ffprobe on PATH and numpy.
"""
import argparse, json, subprocess, sys
import numpy as np


def probe(path):
    out = subprocess.run(
        ["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-select_streams", "v:0", "-show_entries",
         "stream=width,height,avg_frame_rate", "-of", "json", path],
        capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout
    s = json.loads(out)["streams"][0]
    num, den = s["avg_frame_rate"].split("/")
    return int(s["width"]), int(s["height"]), float(num) / float(den)


def frames(path, w, h):
    cmd = ["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", path, "-an", "-vf",
           f"scale={w}:{h}:flags=area", "-pix_fmt", "rgb24", "-f", "rawvideo", "-"]
    raw = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    n = len(raw) // (w * h * 3)
    return np.frombuffer(raw[: n * w * h * 3], np.uint8).reshape(n, h, w, 3).astype(np.int16)


def keyframes(path):
    """Indices of I-frames. Low-bitrate encodes 'pulse' on every keyframe,
    which looks like a small skip but is just the encoder refreshing detail."""
    out = subprocess.run(
        ["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-select_streams", "v:0", "-show_entries",
         "frame=pict_type", "-of", "csv=p=0", path],
        capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout.split()
    return {i for i, t in enumerate(out) if t.strip(",") == "I"}


def diff(a, b):
    return float(np.abs(a - b).mean())


def analyse(path, small_w=36, spike=4.0, floor=6.0, freeze_ratio=0.1, min_freeze_s=0.3):
    W, H, fps = probe(path)
    small_h = max(2, round(small_w * H / W / 2) * 2)
    f = frames(path, small_w, small_h)
    n = len(f)
    kf = keyframes(path)
    min_freeze = max(2, int(round(min_freeze_s * fps)))
    d = np.zeros(n)
    for i in range(1, n):
        d[i] = diff(f[i], f[i - 1])
    # typical motion around each frame: median of a 1-second window, excluding frame 0
    win = max(5, int(round(fps)))
    base = np.zeros(n)
    for i in range(1, n):
        lo, hi = max(1, i - win), min(n, i + win + 1)
        base[i] = np.median(d[lo:hi])
    typical = float(np.median(d[1:])) if n > 1 else 0.0
    events, i = [], 1
    is_spike = lambda k: d[k] > max(spike * base[k], floor)
    while i < n:
        if is_spike(i):
            # flash: spike in, spike out within 3 frames, and the frames either side match
            back = None
            for k in range(1, 4):
                j = i + k
                if j < n and is_spike(j) and diff(f[i - 1], f[j]) < max(spike * base[i], floor) / 2:
                    back = j
                    break
            if back:
                events.append({"type": "flash", "frame": i, "frames": back - i,
                               "time": round(i / fps, 3), "diff": round(float(d[i]), 2)})
                i = back + 1
                continue
            # does the picture stay changed? compare a frame before with a frame after
            after = min(n - 1, i + 2)
            kind = "cut" if diff(f[i - 1], f[after]) > max(spike * base[i], floor) else "jump"
            events.append({"type": kind, "frame": i, "time": round(i / fps, 3),
                           "diff": round(float(d[i]), 2), "typical": round(float(base[i]), 2)})
        elif d[i] < freeze_ratio * max(typical, 1e-6):
            j = i
            while j < n and d[j] < freeze_ratio * max(typical, 1e-6):
                j += 1
            if j - i + 1 >= min_freeze:
                events.append({"type": "freeze", "frame": i - 1, "frames": j - i + 1,
                               "time": round((i - 1) / fps, 3),
                               "seconds": round((j - i + 1) / fps, 3)})
            i = j
            continue
        elif d[i] > max(2.5 * base[i], 1.5 * typical) and d[i] > 1.0:
            events.append({"type": "keyframe" if i in kf else "skip", "frame": i, "time": round(i / fps, 3),
                           "diff": round(float(d[i]), 2), "typical": round(float(base[i]), 2)})
        i += 1
    return {"file": path, "frames": n, "fps": round(fps, 3), "size": f"{W}x{H}",
            "typical_diff": round(typical, 3), "max_diff": round(float(d.max()), 2),
            "events": events}, d


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.split("\n")[0])
    ap.add_argument("clip")
    ap.add_argument("--json", action="store_true")
    ap.add_argument("--csv")
    ap.add_argument("--width", type=int, default=36, help="analysis width in px (smaller = less grain)")
    ap.add_argument("--min-freeze", type=float, default=0.3, help="seconds of no change that count as a freeze")
    ap.add_argument("--spike", type=float, default=4.0, help="x typical motion that counts as a spike")
    a = ap.parse_args()
    try:
        rep, d = analyse(a.clip, small_w=a.width, spike=a.spike, min_freeze_s=a.min_freeze)
    except (subprocess.CalledProcessError, KeyError, IndexError, ValueError) as e:
        print(f"could not read {a.clip}: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    if a.csv:
        with open(a.csv, "w") as fh:
            fh.write("frame,time,diff\n")
            for i, v in enumerate(d):
                fh.write(f"{i},{i / rep['fps']:.3f},{v:.3f}\n")
    if a.json:
        print(json.dumps(rep, indent=2))
    else:
        print(f"{rep['file']}: {rep['frames']} frames @ {rep['fps']} fps, {rep['size']}, "
              f"typical frame-to-frame diff {rep['typical_diff']}, max {rep['max_diff']}")
        if not rep["events"]:
            print("  no cuts, flashes, freezes or skips found")
        for e in rep["events"]:
            extra = {k: v for k, v in e.items() if k not in ("type", "frame", "time")}
            print(f"  {e['type']:6} at {e['time']:6.3f}s (frame {e['frame']})  {extra}")
    real = [e for e in rep["events"] if e["type"] != "keyframe"]
    if any(e["type"] == "keyframe" for e in rep["events"]):
        print("  (keyframe = small pulse on an I-frame, usually encoder refresh; not counted)")
    return 1 if real else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

Run it:

python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4          # report, exit 1 if anything found
python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4 --json   # for CI or a batch script
python3 jumpcheck.py clip.mp4 --csv diffs.csv   # plot the curve yourself

Planting defects to test it

You can't trust a detector you've only run on clean clips. make_glitch.sh takes any clip and plants one known defect at a known frame:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Make a test copy of a clip with one known defect, to check a jump detector.
#   ./make_glitch.sh in.mp4 cut|flash|freeze|drop|lowbitrate N out.mp4
#   cut        N ignored: from 4 s on, the picture is flipped and hue-rotated (a "different shot")
#   flash      N white frames starting at frame 90
#   freeze     frame 150 held for N frames (same total length)
#   drop       N frames removed starting at frame 120 (clip gets shorter, motion jumps)
#   lowbitrate N ignored: CRF 38 with a keyframe every 30 frames (encoder pulse, not a defect)
set -euo pipefail
in=$1; kind=$2; n=$3; out=$4
enc=(-c:v libx264 -preset veryfast -crf 20 -pix_fmt yuv420p)
case $kind in
  cut) ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$in" -filter_complex \
        "[0:v]split[a][b];[a]trim=0:4,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS[a2];[b]trim=4,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS,vflip,hue=h=120[b2];[a2][b2]concat=n=2:v=1:a=0,fps=30[v]" \
        -map "[v]" -map 0:a? "${enc[@]}" -c:a copy "$out" ;;
  flash) ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$in" -vf "drawbox=0:0:iw:ih:color=white:t=fill:enable='between(n,90,$((90+n-1)))'" \
        "${enc[@]}" -c:a copy "$out" ;;
  freeze) ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$in" -filter_complex "[0:v]split[a][b];[a][b]freezeframes=first=150:last=$((150+n-1)):replace=150[v]" \
        -map "[v]" -map 0:a? "${enc[@]}" -c:a copy "$out" ;;
  drop) ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$in" -vf "select='not(between(n,120,$((120+n-1))))',setpts=N/30/TB" -an -r 30 "${enc[@]}" "$out" ;;
  lowbitrate) ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$in" -c:v libx264 -preset veryfast -crf 38 -g 30 -pix_fmt yuv420p -c:a copy "$out" ;;
  *) echo "unknown kind $kind" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac
echo "wrote $out ($kind $n)"

The base clip comes from a small synthetic generator (make_field_test_clip.sh: gradient sky, noisy field, red box with white text swaying on a sine, beeps over a hum). It's in the same folder as the scripts.

Results

Same base clip, one defect at a time:

Test clip jumpcheck.py found Exit
clean clip, grain 18 nothing (typical diff 1.07, max 1.54) 0
hard cut at 4.0 s cut at frame 120, diff 102.3 vs local 1.12 1
1 white frame at 3.0 s flash at frame 90, 1 frame 1
2 white frames at 3.0 s flash at frame 90, 2 frames 1
frame 150 held 15 frames freeze at 5.0 s, 0.5 s 1
15 frames dropped at 4.0 s skip at frame 120, diff 4.06 vs 1.11 1
clean clip, no grain nothing (typical 0.245) 0
clean clip scaled to 480x854 nothing 0
clean clip re-encoded CRF 38, keyframe every 30 7 keyframe pulses listed, not counted 0
file that doesn't exist error message 2

For comparison: ffmpeg's scdet

ffmpeg ships a scene-change filter, so the obvious question is why not just use it:

ffmpeg -i clip.mp4 -vf "scdet=threshold=10,metadata=print:file=scd.txt" -f null -

On the same planted clips at threshold=10:

Defect Highest lavfi.scd.score Flagged?
clean 0.17 no
hard cut 24.5 (frame 120) yes
1 white frame 36.8 (frame 90) yes, but only the entry. The exit frame scored low, so it looks just like a cut
15-frame freeze 2.4 no
15 dropped frames 0.9 no

That isn't a bug. scdet is built to find scene changes, and its score is roughly "how much did the frame difference jump compared with the previous difference". The return from a flash is a big difference right after another big difference, so it scores low. Freezes and small skips aren't scene changes at all. If all you need is real cuts, scdet is fine. To tell a flash from a cut, or catch the quieter defects, you need the raw curve.

Two false alarms that shaped the defaults

1. Low-bitrate keyframe "pulses." I re-encoded the clean clip at CRF 38 with a keyframe every 30 frames. The first version of the script reported seven "skips" at frames 29, 58, 87 and so on, exactly 29 frames apart. ffprobe -show_entries frame=pict_type showed an I-frame at every one of them. At low bitrate, every keyframe refreshes detail the P-frames had smeared away, and that registers as a small jump. The script now asks ffprobe for I-frame positions, labels those events keyframe and leaves them out of the exit code.

The cost of that choice is that a real skip landing on a keyframe gets hidden. This happened once in the dataset grid I mention below. Before I made the test clip deterministic, a 10-frame drop got labelled keyframe because x264 had put an I-frame right at the jump. If you have a clip that already feels wrong, also read the keyframe lines.

2. Slow motion looks like a freeze. With grain turned off, the test banner moves less than a pixel per frame at the slow ends of its sway. After encoding, some frames come out identical. The first version flagged eight "freezes" of 3-7 frames (0.1-0.23 s) in a perfectly fine clip. Raising the minimum to 0.3 s removed all of them and still caught the planted 15-frame freeze. A 0.1 s pause in an AI clip is rarely what people mean by "it froze".

Where it stops working

  • Tiny skips are invisible. On the grainy clip, dropping 1, 2 or 5 frames wasn't detected. The motion jump is smaller than the grain. On the grain-free clip, 5 dropped frames were caught (diff 1.59 vs typical 0.244) but 1-2 weren't. Freezes of 3 and 6 frames were not reported (by design, under 0.3 s); 9 and 15 were. A full grid of these cases is in the dataset linked at the end.
  • A cut to a similar-looking shot can slip through. My cut fixture flips the picture and rotates the hue, so it's an obvious change. A cut between two nearly identical framings won't produce a big spike.
  • The freeze after-effect. When a freeze ends, the motion catches up in one frame. On the grain-free clip that catch-up was also reported as a skip. It isn't a second defect, just the other end of the same freeze.
  • Thresholds were tuned on synthetic clips. Real footage with camera shake will need --spike raised.

What to do with the list

  • It's your own edit. Look at the reported frame first. Flashes and freezes usually come from a transition, a bad cut point or a dropped frame in the export. Trim with frame accuracy (re-encode, don't stream-copy) and run the check again.
  • The clip came out of the generator like that. The studio's help page separates a failed generation from one that looks wrong. Looking different from your photo isn't a failed order on its own. If you write to support, a frame number and a timestamp make the report concrete. The address is on the help page.

title: osFoundry는 왜 Codex CLI에 변경을 푸시하지 않고 리소스마다 커서로 폴링하게 할까
summary:
osFoundry MCP 서버에서 "뭔가 바뀌면 알고 싶은" 클라이언트가 쓸 수 있는 걸 이 Mac에서 토큰 없이 전부 두드려 봤다.

$ uv run --with tiktoken --with jsonschema python3 watch_sim.py
== Part 1: live wire, 8 calls each, ms ==
initialize                   HTTP 200  median  414.7  p90  757.8
tools/list                   HTTP 200  median  606.8  p90  716.7
resources/subscribe          HTTP 200  median  450.6  p90  550.2
GET (stream)                 HTTP 405  median  423.9  p90  475.4
tools/call poll (no token)   HTTP 401  median  322.0  p90  463.9
initialize capabilities: {"tools": {"listChanged": false}}
resources/subscribe -> {"code": -32601, "message": "Method not found"}
GET body -> ''
poll without token -> isError True | Authentication required
rate limit headers: limit 2000, reset in 61 s

푸시 경로는 세 개 다 닫혀 있다. initialize가 선언하는 건 tools뿐이고 그마저 listChanged: false라서, 툴 목록이 바뀌어도 알려 주지 않는다. resources/subscribe는 "Method not found"다. Streamable HTTP 서버라면 서버→클라이언트 스트림을 열어 줄 MCP URL로의 GET은 405를 돌려준다. 남는 건 읽기 전용 툴 하나뿐이다.

{"name": "poll_resource_events",
 "description": "Resume from an event sequence for one granted channel, Note, knowledge base, record, or session.",
 "inputSchema": {"properties": {
     "resource_type": {"enum": ["message_channel", "note", "knowledge_base", "record_channel", "room",
                                "gitnest_repository", "agent_session", "team_session", "loop_session",
                                "graph_session"]},
     "resource_id": {"type": "string"},
     "after_sequence": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 0},
     "limit": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 100}},
   "required": ["resource_type", "resource_id"], "additionalProperties": false},
 "annotations": {"readOnlyHint": true, "openWorldHint": false, "destructiveHint": false},
 "securitySchemes": [{"type": "oauth2", "scopes": ["osfoundry:read"]}]}

핵심은 "one granted"와 "resume from an event sequence" 두 표현이다. 이 글에서는 이 두 표현을 클라이언트 쪽을 Python으로 다시 만들어서 확인한다. 이 Mac에는 codex 바이너리가 없어서 클라이언트 역할은 스크립트가 했다. osFoundry 서버 코드는 공개돼 있지 않다. Part 1과 2는 라이브 서버고, Part 3은 재현이라 응답 모양과 활동 빈도는 재현 쪽에서 정한 값이다.

왜 푸시가 아니라 폴링일까, 특히 Codex라면

Codex CLI는 상주 프로세스가 아니다. 실행하면 돌고, 턴 하나를 처리하고, 끝나거나 사용자 입력을 기다린다. 푸시를 받으려면 세션과 세션 사이에도 누군가 귀를 열고 있어야 하는데, 노트북에선 대개 아무도 없다. 시퀀스 커서는 이런 생활 방식에 딱 맞는다. 클라이언트는 리소스마다 정수 하나만 들고 있다가, 내키는 때 돌아와서 그 뒤로 무슨 일이 있었는지 물으면 된다.

위의 ms 숫자는 일본에서 Apple M1으로 잰 거라 서버보다 경로 얘기에 가깝다. 더 중요한 건 레이트 리밋 헤더다. 인증 안 된 응답에 X-RateLimit-Limit: 2000이 붙고, 리셋은 61초쯤 뒤다. 로그인한 클라이언트도 같은 한도인지는 확인 안 했다. 그래도 리소스 30개를 30초마다 폴링해 봐야 분당 60요청이다. Codex로 변경을 지켜볼 때 발목을 잡는 건 서버 부하가 아니라 Codex 자신의 턴 수다. 폴링 한 번이 곧 모델이 툴을 부르고 결과를 읽는 한 턴이다.

폴링해도 되는 대상은 어떻게 찾을까

호출 두 개면 되고, 스키마만 봐도 설계 의도가 꽤 드러난다.

list_granted_resources   osfoundry:read  ro=True required=[] props=[]
list_project_resources   osfoundry:read  ro=True required=['project_id', 'resource_type'] props=['project_id', 'resource_type', 'search', 'offset', 'limit']
poll_resource_events     osfoundry:read  ro=True required=['resource_type', 'resource_id'] props=['resource_type', 'resource_id', 'after_sequence', 'limit']
59 tools on server; these three = 591 of 12662 tokens (4.7%, cl100k_base)
poll_resource_events types: 10 | list_project_resources types: 9 | only pollable: ['graph_session']

list_granted_resources는 인자를 하나도 안 받고, 억지로 넣으면 스키마가 튕긴다.

list_granted_resources   no arguments           ok
list_granted_resources   project_id passed      REJECT additionalProperties

클라이언트가 뭔가를 요청하는 툴이 아니라, 서버가 "네가 가진 건 이거다"라고 알려 주는 툴이다. initialize의 instructions도 "Use list_granted_resources first."로 시작한다. 돌아오는 건 연결에 추가된 프로젝트와 개별로 허용된 리소스다. 웹 클라이언트(ExternalAssistantsPanel.tsx)로 치면 Projects 영역과 "Older individual access" 영역이다.

list_project_resources는 resource_type이 필수다. "이 프로젝트 안에 있는 거 전부" 같은 목록은 없어서, 전체를 파악하려면 타입마다 한 번씩 아홉 번 불러야 한다. 한 타입에 50개가 넘으면(limit 최대 50, offset으로 페이지 넘김) 더 늘어난다. 설명문에는 프로젝트 단위 접근의 유일한 예외도 적혀 있다. "Ordinary Message channels require a separate invitation."

커서는 왜 서버가 아니라 클라이언트가 들고 있을까

osFoundry에는 두 방식이 다 있다. 에이전트 네트워크의 wait_for_messages는 커서를 서버가 들고 있어 준다. "Without after_sequence it resumes where your last call stopped"라고 돼 있고, timeout_s로 최대 50초까지 롱 폴링도 된다. poll_resource_events에는 둘 다 없다. timeout_s는 튕기고 설명엔 "resume from"뿐이니, 번호는 클라이언트가 챙겨 와야 한다.

wait_for_messages props: ['after_sequence', 'timeout_s', 'limit'] timeout_s max 50 | poll_resource_events has timeout: False
poll_resource_events     timeout_s 30           REJECT additionalProperties

서버가 커서를 들고 있으면 듣는 쪽이 하나일 땐 편하다. 그런데 연결 하나를 클라이언트 둘이 같이 쓰면 깨진다. 같은 로그인으로 터미널 두 개에서 Codex를 열면 딱 그 상황이다. 재현에서 채널 이벤트 600개를, 랜덤하게 번갈아 폴링하는 터미널 두 개에 흘려 봤다.

two terminals, client cursor: A saw 600/600, B saw 600/600
two terminals, server cursor: A saw 305/600, B saw 295/600

연결마다 서버가 커서를 하나 들고 있으면, 한쪽이 커서를 밀 때마다 다른 쪽은 그만큼 놓쳐서 각자 절반 정도만 본다. 요청에 after_sequence를 넣는 방식이면 둘 다 전부 보고, 서버는 읽는 쪽 상태를 하나도 안 들고 있어도 된다. 여러 툴이 제각각 읽어 가는 리소스 로그라면 커서 주인은 클라이언트가 맞다.

스키마상 after_sequence는 필수가 아니지만, 빼면 어떻게 되는지는 어디에도 안 적혀 있다. 거기 기대지 말자. 번호를 저장해 두고 매번 보내는 게 안전하다.

페이지가 꽉 차면 몇 번 불러야 할까

limit은 100이 끝이다. 대량 임포트 뒤라면 노트 하나에 이벤트가 수백 개 쌓여 있을 수 있다. 마지막 시퀀스부터 다시 부르고, 페이지가 꽉 차지 않은 채로 올 때까지 반복해서 비운다.

burst of 350 events, limit 100:  4 calls to drain, cursor ends at 350
burst of 350 events, limit  50:  7 calls to drain, cursor ends at 350
burst of 350 events, limit  20: 18 calls to drain, cursor ends at 350

100으로 부르면 된다. 재현에서 응답 크기는 빈 페이지가 17토큰, 이벤트 하나짜리가 41토큰이었다(cl100k_base). 모양은 재현 쪽 거지 osFoundry 게 아니지만, 자릿수 감은 충분하다. 빈 폴링은 읽는 비용이 싸고, 폴링 비용은 거의 턴 수로 정해진다.

리소스 30개를 얼마 간격으로 폴링해야 할까

재현에서는 프로젝트 하나에 목록으로 뽑을 수 있는 아홉 타입의 리소스 30개를 두고 활동량을 한쪽으로 몰았다. 바쁜 게 3개(분당 이벤트 1개), 적당한 게 7개(10분에 1개), 조용한 게 20개(2시간에 1개). 빈도는 가정이다. 8시간짜리 하루를 시드 5개로, 가상 시계 위에서 돌렸다.

every 30 s, all 30                 calls/hour   3600  empty  94.7%  seen late median   14.9 s  p90   27.0 s  max     30 s  (1843 events/day)
every 5 min, all 30                calls/hour    360  empty  78.0%  seen late median  150.9 s  p90  271.1 s  max    300 s  (1843 events/day)
30 s, x2 when empty, cap 10 min    calls/hour    502  empty  70.2%  seen late median   34.9 s  p90  206.4 s  max    599 s  (1843 events/day)
30 s, x2 when empty, cap 30 min    calls/hour    420  empty  65.3%  seen late median   35.6 s  p90  238.4 s  max   1799 s  (1843 events/day)
server window for comparison: 2000 requests per ~61 s

고정 30초는 빠르지만 95%가 헛방이다. 시간당 3,600번 부르고 거의 다 비어 있다. 고정 5분은 싸지만, 바쁜 채널까지 포함해서 전부 느리다. 리소스별 백오프(빈 폴링마다 그 리소스의 간격을 두 배로 늘리고, 이벤트가 오면 처음으로 되돌림)는 호출 수를 싼 쪽에 가깝게 맞추면서 지연 중앙값은 빠른 쪽에 가깝게 유지한다. 바쁜 리소스는 30초에 머물고 조용한 것만 멀어지기 때문이다. 대가는 상한값이다. 30분으로 두면 조용한 리소스의 첫 변경은 최대 30분까지 기다릴 수 있다.

Codex 입장에선 이 표가 오히려 타이머를 아예 안 돌릴 이유가 된다. 사람이 "뭐 바뀌었어?"라고 물을 때 저장해 둔 커서로 한 바퀴 돌면, 지켜보는 리소스 하나당 호출 한 번으로 그 시점까지의 변경을 지연 0으로 잡는다. 백오프 표는 Codex든 뭐든 계속 지켜보게 돌려 두는 스크립트를 위한 거다.

오너가 4시간 07분 시점에 프로젝트를 뺐다고 하자. 커서 30개가 전부 이제 못 읽는 리소스를 가리킨다. 문제는 클라이언트가 그걸 언제까지 폴링하느냐다.

타이머로 그랜트를 다시 확인하면 호출이 늘거나, 실패하는 폴링을 수천 번 쌓거나 둘 중 하나다. 처음 거절당한 순간을 "그랜트 다시 읽기" 신호로 쓰면 실패 한 번과 list_granted_resources 호출 한 번이면 끝난다. 그다음 목록에서 사라진 리소스의 커서를 버리면 된다. 나중에 오너가 프로젝트를 다시 넣어 주면 그 리소스들은 처음부터 새로 시작한다.

스키마는 어디서 막을까

나머지 케이스도 라이브 inputSchema에 jsonschema(Draft 2020-12)로 돌려 봤다.

list_project_resources   limit 50               ok
list_project_resources   limit 51               REJECT maximum: limit
list_project_resources   graph_session          REJECT enum: resource_type
list_project_resources   search 101 chars       REJECT maxLength: search
poll_resource_events     no after_sequence      ok
poll_resource_events     graph_session          ok
poll_resource_events     after_sequence -1      REJECT minimum: after_sequence
poll_resource_events     limit 100              ok
poll_resource_events     limit 101              REJECT maximum: limit
poll_resource_events     resource_type project  REJECT enum: resource_type

다들 제일 먼저 해 보는 게 resource_type: "project"다. 프로젝트는 로그를 가진 리소스가 아니라, 리소스를 보이게 해 주는 그랜트 단위다.

스크립트 전체는 M1에서 20.2초 걸렸고, 그중 대부분이 네트워크 호출 40번이었다. 유저 CPU 시간은 0.91초였다.

직접 만든다면

  • 로그는 리소스마다 하나로 두고, 커서는 클라이언트가 들게 한다. 연결 하나를 둘이 읽어도 이벤트를 뺏어 가지 않고, 서버는 읽는 쪽 상태를 저장할 필요가 없다.
  • 그랜트 목록은 인자 없는 전용 툴로 만들고, 클라이언트가 거기서 시작하게 한다. 찾을 수 있는 건 오너가 허용한 것뿐이어야 한다.
  • 페이지 크기에 상한을 두고, 다 비우는 법(마지막 시퀀스부터, 덜 찬 페이지가 올 때까지 다시 부르기)을 정해 둔다.
  • 백오프는 전역이 아니라 리소스별로. 바쁜 건 빠르게, 조용한 건 싸게.
  • 폴링이 처음 거절되면 그랜트를 다시 읽고, 사라진 커서는 재시도하지 말고 버린다.
  • 커서는 이벤트를 처리한 다음에 기록한다. 중간에 죽어도 건너뛰는 게 아니라 다시 읽게 된다.

연결마다 툴이 어떻게 정해지는지는 툴 스코프 페이지, 프로토콜의 짧은 정의는 MCP 용어 설명에 있다.

osFoundry MCP 서버에서 "뭔가 바뀌면 알고 싶은" 클라이언트가 쓸 수 있는 걸 이 Mac에서 토큰 없이 전부 두드려 봤다.

initialize                   HTTP 200  median  414.7  p90  757.8
tools/list                   HTTP 200  median  606.8  p90  716.7
resources/subscribe          HTTP 200  median  450.6  p90  550.2
GET (stream)                 HTTP 405  median  423.9  p90  475.4
tools/call poll (no token)   HTTP 401  median  322.0  p90  463.9
initialize capabilities: {"tools": {"listChanged": false}}

poll without token -> isError True | Authentication required
rate limit headers: limit 2000, reset in 61 s

푸시 경로는 세 개 다 닫혀 있다. initialize가 선언하는 건 tools뿐이고 그마저 listChanged: false라서, 툴 목록이 바뀌어도 알려 주지 않는다. resources/subscribe는 "Method not found"다. Streamable HTTP 서버라면 서버→클라이언트 스트림을 열어 줄 MCP URL로의 GET은 405를 돌려준다. 남는 건 읽기 전용 툴 하나뿐이다.

{"name": "poll_resource_events",
 "description": "Resume from an event sequence for one granted channel, Note, knowledge base, record, or session.",
 "inputSchema": {"properties": {
     "resource_type": {"enum": ["message_channel", "note", "knowledge_base", "record_channel", "room",
                                "gitnest_repository", "agent_session", "team_session", "loop_session",
                                "graph_session"]},
     "resource_id": {"type": "string"},
     "after_sequence": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 0},
     "limit": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 100}},
   "required": ["resource_type", "resource_id"], "additionalProperties": false},

 "securitySchemes": [{"type": "oauth2", "scopes": ["osfoundry:read"]}]}

Codex CLI는 상주 프로세스가 아니다. 실행하면 돌고, 턴 하나를 처리하고, 끝나거나 사용자 입력을 기다린다. 푸시를 받으려면 세션과 세션 사이에도 누군가 귀를 열고 있어야 하는데, 노트북에선 대개 아무도 없다. 시퀀스 커서는 이런 생활 방식에 딱 맞는다. 클라이언트는 리소스마다 정수 하나만 들고 있다가, 내키는 때 돌아와서 그 뒤로 무슨 일이 있었는지 물으면 된다.

위의 ms 숫자는 일본에서 Apple M1으로 잰 거라 서버보다 경로 얘기에 가깝다. 더 중요한 건 레이트 리밋 헤더다. 인증 안 된 응답에 X-RateLimit-Limit: 2000이 붙고, 리셋은 61초쯤 뒤다. 로그인한 클라이언트도 같은 한도인지는 확인 안 했다. 그래도 리소스 30개를 30초마다 폴링해 봐야 분당 60요청이다. Codex로 변경을 지켜볼 때 발목을 잡는 건 서버 부하가 아니라 Codex 자신의 턴 수다. 폴링 한 번이 곧 모델이 툴을 부르고 결과를 읽는 한 턴이다.

100으로 부르면 된다. 재현에서 응답 크기는 빈 페이지가 17토큰, 이벤트 하나짜리가 41토큰이었다(cl100k_base). 모양은 재현 쪽 거지 osFoundry 게 아니지만, 자릿수 감은 충분하다. 빈 폴링은 읽는 비용이 싸고, 폴링 비용은 거의 턴 수로 정해진다.

고정 30초는 빠르지만 95%가 헛방이다. 시간당 3,600번 부르고 거의 다 비어 있다. 고정 5분은 싸지만, 바쁜 채널까지 포함해서 전부 느리다. 리소스별 백오프(빈 폴링마다 그 리소스의 간격을 두 배로 늘리고, 이벤트가 오면 처음으로 되돌림)는 호출 수를 싼 쪽에 가깝게 맞추면서 지연 중앙값은 빠른 쪽에 가깝게 유지한다. 바쁜 리소스는 30초에 머물고 조용한 것만 멀어지기 때문이다. 대가는 상한값이다. 30분으로 두면 조용한 리소스의 첫 변경은 최대 30분까지 기다릴 수 있다.

스크립트 전체는 M1에서 20.2초 걸렸고, 그중 대부분이 네트워크 호출 40번이었다. 유저 CPU 시간은 0.91초였다.

직접 만든다면

  • 로그는 리소스마다 하나로 두고, 커서는 클라이언트가 들게 한다. 연결 하나를 둘이 읽어도 이벤트를 뺏어 가지 않고, 서버는 읽는 쪽 상태를 저장할 필요가 없다.

title: A small offline check for route data before making a travel animation
summary:
A map animation makes movement look continuous, even when the underlying record is sparse. That visual effect can be useful for storytelling, but it can also hide missing samples, time-zone mistakes, and values that do not represent valid coordinates. Before turning an exported route into a public clip, it helps to run a few small checks and then review the map itself.

This article builds an offline Python check for a deliberately simple CSV format. It does not parse the Google Timeline export format, reconstruct a route, prove where anyone was, or determine whether a location can safely be shared. The examples and tests use synthetic values. I am associated with Timeline Visualizer, and AI assisted in drafting this article and code. Timeline Visualizer is a browser-based google timeline visualizer that turns exported location history into an animated travel video. It offers route customization and MP4 export; custom music is part of the optional Pro upgrade. This standalone code is not a feature of the product or an integration with it.

Choose a narrow input contract

The example accepts rows with three fields: lat, lon, and timestamp. Latitude and longitude are decimal degrees. The timestamp is an ISO 8601 value with an explicit UTC offset, such as 2025-05-08T09:00:00+00:00. A trailing Z is also accepted as UTC. These fields are a teaching format, not a claim about the fields present in a particular service's export.

A real conversion layer needs its own documentation and tests. If an input represents coordinates as integers scaled by a power of ten, for example, those values must be converted correctly before this checker receives them. If a timestamp is a Unix epoch, it must be converted to an offset-aware value deliberately. Guessing a format from a number's length can produce plausible but incorrect coordinates, so keep source parsing separate from validation.

The tool returns row numbers and short warning labels. It deliberately avoids printing the actual coordinates. That reduces accidental exposure in console output, although row numbers can still reveal information when combined with the original file. Treat both the input and any report as private. The function operates on data already in memory and makes no network calls; that does not make a machine or its backups automatically secure.

A small checker 

import csv
import math
from datetime import datetime


def audit(rows, gap_minutes=120):
    issues = []
    previous = None
    for number, row in enumerate(rows, 1):
        try:
            lat, lon = float(row['lat']), float(row['lon'])
            stamp = datetime.fromisoformat(
                row['timestamp'].replace('Z', '+00:00')
            )
            if stamp.utcoffset() is None:
                raise ValueError('timestamp must include offset')
            if not (math.isfinite(lat) and math.isfinite(lon)
                    and -90 <= lat <= 90 and -180 <= lon <= 180):
                raise ValueError('invalid coordinate')
        except (KeyError, TypeError, ValueError):
            issues.append((number, 'invalid row'))
            previous = None
            continue
        if previous is not None:
            delta = (stamp - previous).total_seconds() / 60
            if delta < 0:
                issues.append((number, 'out of order'))
            elif delta > gap_minutes:
                issues.append((number, 'large time gap'))
        previous = stamp
    return issues


def read_csv(path):
    with open(path, encoding='utf-8', newline='') as handle:
        return list(csv.DictReader(handle))

The bounds check rejects values outside the possible latitude and longitude ranges. math.isfinite matters because Python accepts strings such as nan and inf as floating-point values; those are not usable positions. A numeric value inside the range can still be wrong. Swapped latitude and longitude may pass, and a plausible coordinate can belong to the wrong city. This code reports basic validity, not geographic truth.

The ordering check compares each valid timestamp to the previous valid timestamp. A negative interval is flagged as out of order. An interval strictly greater than the chosen threshold is flagged as a large time gap. Two points exactly 120 minutes apart are not flagged under the default setting. A gap is a prompt to inspect the source, not proof that a device failed or that a traveler moved directly between the two points.

When a row is invalid, the code clears the previous timestamp. The next valid row begins a new comparison sequence. This avoids pretending that the checker knows how to bridge a malformed row. Depending on the application, a different policy might be appropriate, but it should be explicit and covered by tests. For example, a production pipeline may want a separate warning that a comparison was interrupted.

Exercise the boundary cases

The following small tests use fabricated coordinates and times. Save the checker as route_audit.py and run this snippet in the same directory. They test the code shown above, not the Timeline Visualizer product or any real export.

from route_audit import audit


def row(lat, lon, stamp):
    return {'lat': lat, 'lon': lon, 'timestamp': stamp}


a = '2025-05-08T09:00:00+00:00'
b = '2025-05-08T09:30:00+00:00'
c = '2025-05-08T13:00:00+00:00'

assert audit([row('48', '2', a), row('48.1', '2.1', b)]) == []
assert audit([row('48', '2', a), row('48', '2', c)]) == [(2, 'large time gap')]
assert audit([row('48', '2', b), row('48', '2', a)]) == [(2, 'out of order')]
assert audit([row('nan', '2', a)]) == [(1, 'invalid row')]
assert audit([row('91', '2', a)]) == [(1, 'invalid row')]
assert audit([row('48', '2', '2025-05-08T09:00:00')]) == [(1, 'invalid row')]
assert audit([row('48', '2', a), {}, row('48', '2', c)]) == [(2, 'invalid row')]
assert audit([
    row('48', '2', '2025-05-08T09:00:00Z'),
    row('48', '2', '2025-05-08T11:00:00+02:00'),
]) == []
print('8 synthetic assertions passed')

These eight assertions passed locally against the accompanying example. The last test uses two representations of the same instant with different offsets. Python compares aware datetimes by instant, so the interval is zero. The test is useful because sorting timestamp strings lexicographically is not generally a safe substitute for parsing offsets. Local dates are still important for a human itinerary, but that is a separate presentation decision.

Decide what a warning means

A warning should lead to a question, not an automatic correction. For a large gap, inspect the original record and any itinerary information you already have. It may correspond to a device being offline, but it may also be an intentional stop. For out-of-order rows, determine whether the file was meant to be ordered by recording time, import order, or another field. Sorting blindly can obscure an upstream issue or change the intended sequence.

Consider the threshold in context. Two hours may be reasonable for a dense city walk and unhelpful for a route sampled only a few times per day. Pass a different gap_minutes value when the sampling policy is known, and record that choice with the review. This example does not validate the threshold itself; a production implementation should reject negative, non-finite, or otherwise inappropriate settings and return structured errors suitable for its caller.

Do not use a single numeric check as a privacy guarantee. A valid point may be a home, school, workplace, or medical location. A seemingly broad map can identify a person through a distinctive combination of places and times. Review the route and audience explicitly, remove unnecessary segments, obtain consent when others are represented, and remember that a shared video can be copied beyond the initial recipients.

Turn checks into a reviewable workflow

Keep the raw export private and work on a copy. Run validation before selecting a visual style, then make a short list of warnings to inspect. Check the first and last locations, the order of major stops, missing intervals, and any labels visible at the intended playback size. If the source is uncertain, leave a gap or describe the uncertainty instead of drawing a confident line that the data does not support.

After editing, play the actual exported video from start to finish. Confirm that the map scale provides enough context without exposing more than the audience needs. If music is included, make sure the license covers the intended use. If a video will be compressed by a messaging or social platform, check the compressed copy as well as the original. A clear opening frame and a short pause at an important stop can do more for comprehension than additional motion effects.

The boundary between data quality, privacy, and presentation is important. The Python function only catches a few mechanical problems. A person still needs to decide what the journey is meant to communicate and what should remain private. A small, well-documented checker is valuable precisely because its limitations are visible: it helps organize review without replacing judgment or presenting an animation as authoritative evidence.

title: Building Safer AI Memory: Inside RagLeap Memory v0.3.1
summary:
Encrypted memory export, AES-256-GCM, tamper detection, and the engineering work behind safer memory portability.

AI systems are becoming increasingly dependent on persistent memory.

An AI employee needs to retain useful context across tasks, retrieve relevant information, and operate within clearly defined boundaries. But memory is not just about storing information. It also involves protecting that information when it moves between systems.

With RagLeap Memory v0.3.1, we've taken another step towards building a stronger, security-conscious memory infrastructure for open-source AI employees.

This release introduces optional encrypted memory export and import, powered by AES-256-GCM through ragleap-security.

This article explains what changed, how the encryption works, what we tested, and — just as importantly — what this release does not claim to protect.

1. Why encrypted memory portability matters

Memory portability is useful when operators need to:

  • Move memory exports between environments.
  • Back up selected memory scopes.
  • Transfer memory data securely.
  • Preserve useful context across deployments.
  • Manage memory exports with stronger confidentiality guarantees.

However, a portable memory file can contain sensitive information.

A plain export may be convenient, but anyone who obtains that file could potentially inspect its contents.

RagLeap Memory 0.3.1 adds an optional encryption layer to exported memory files while preserving the existing plain-export behaviour for users who do not enable encryption.

The goal is straightforward: make memory portability safer without unexpectedly changing existing workflows.

2. AES-256-GCM encrypted exports

The new encryption capability uses AES-256-GCM through the ragleap-security package.

The memory package provides the export/import workflow, while the security package handles the underlying encryption.

Install the optional cryptography dependency:

pip install "ragleap-memory[crypto]==0.3.1"

The base package remains available without the optional extra:

pip install ragleap-memory==0.3.1

If encryption is requested without the optional dependency, the package raises an error explaining which extra is required.

This keeps the encryption dependency optional and avoids changing the behaviour of installations that do not need it.

3. New encryption APIs

Version 0.3.1 adds optional encryption and decryption parameters to the existing file and stream APIs.

The new export signature is:

export_file(
    scope,
    path,
    encrypt_with=None,
    passphrase=None,
    context=None,
)

Import operations support:

import_file(
    ...,
    decrypt_with=None,
    passphrase=None,
    context=None,
)

And the same decryption options are available through import_stream.

The implementation supports:

  • Key for encryption and decryption.
  • KeyRing for key selection and rotation workflows.
  • Passphrase-based encryption using scrypt-derived keys.
  • Context-bound encrypted exports.

Passphrase derivation happens once per file rather than once per individual memory entry.

This provides flexibility for different operational requirements without forcing every user into one key-management approach.

4. Tamper detection and context binding

Encryption alone is not the complete story.

The release also strengthens the relationship between encrypted entries and their original export.

Each encrypted line is bound to:

  • A fixed cryptographic label.
  • The SHA-256 hash of the exact header line.
  • Its position in the export.
  • The supplied context.

This means changes to encrypted data, moving entries, duplicating entries, or attempting to reuse entries across different export contexts will cause decryption to fail.

Incorrect keys or contexts also result in decryption failure.

The import process checks the expected entry count, so dropped or additional lines are rejected.

Errors are reported with the relevant line number rather than silently accepting corrupted data.

These checks are intended to make accidental modification and tampering detectable.

5. No silent downgrade between encrypted and plain exports

A security-sensitive import operation should not silently change its interpretation of a file.

RagLeap Memory 0.3.1 explicitly distinguishes encrypted and plain exports.

The new behaviour includes:

  • Encrypted exports require the appropriate decryption key or passphrase.
  • Supplying encryption credentials for a plain export causes the import to refuse it.
  • Unsupported header versions are rejected.
  • Version 2 headers identify encrypted exports.
  • Existing version 1 plain exports continue to work.

Importantly, existing calls without the new arguments retain their 0.3.0 behaviour.

This makes the release additive rather than a breaking change for existing users.

6. Existing import safeguards remain in place

Decryption does not bypass the existing memory import controls.

After decryption, data still passes through the established import path, including:

  • Trust limits.
  • Scope validation.
  • Quotas.
  • Size limits.
  • A single database transaction.
  • Existing import safety checks.

The principle is important: encryption should protect the exported file, but it should not become a shortcut around the controls governing what enters the memory system.

7. Testing beyond ordinary unit tests

Security-sensitive changes require more than checking whether encryption and decryption work in a basic example.

For this release, we performed several layers of verification.

Test results:

Verification Result
VPS test suite, Python 3.10 532 passed
Sandbox test suite, Python 3.10 532 passed
Sandbox test suite, Python 3.12 532 passed
Mutation testing 232/232 caught
GitHub CI checks on implementation PR 55/55 passed

Mutation testing deliberately introduces changes into the implementation to determine whether the tests detect them.

In this release, all 232 tested mutations were detected in the reported sandbox runs.

We also performed release-artifact verification:

  • The five Python files in the published wheel were compared with the source at the release tag.
  • Fresh installations were tested with and without the optional crypto extra.
  • The source distribution test suite was run against the installed wheel.
  • A real database export created using RagLeap Memory 0.3.0 was successfully opened and imported.
  • RagLeap Memory 0.3.0 rejected a 0.3.1 encrypted export with the expected unsupported-version behaviour.

The published wheel and source distribution were also checked against their recorded SHA-256 digests and release provenance.

These checks provide evidence that the published package corresponds to the tested release source.

8. Important security limitations

We want to be precise about what this release protects.

Encrypted export files are protected — not the entire memory environment.

The current implementation does not encrypt:

  • The underlying SQLite database.
  • Process memory while exporting or importing.
  • Other application data outside the exported file.

There are additional limitations:

  • The export header reveals the number of entries.
  • Encrypted line lengths reveal approximate entry sizes.
  • Anyone possessing the appropriate key can read or forge an export.
  • Replaying an older valid export is not detected by this release.
  • Decrypted content remains untrusted input and must still pass the import safeguards.
  • No independent security audit has been performed.

Large imports are also subject to the configured size limit, which defaults to 64 MiB.

We believe transparent security boundaries are essential. Encryption should not be presented as a guarantee that every part of a memory system is secure.

9. Where this fits into RagLeap's memory direction

RagLeap is building an open-source, self-hosted AI employee platform.

Our memory direction is not simply about sharing personal context between different chat applications.

We are working towards a stronger memory infrastructure that can support AI employees and enterprise workflows.

That requires several capabilities to work together:

  • Persistent and structured memory.
  • Scoped access and isolation.
  • Reliable retrieval.
  • Security and controlled data portability.
  • Memory governance and lifecycle management.
  • Integration with the wider AI employee architecture.

RagLeap Memory 0.3.1 is one step in that direction.

It does not complete the enterprise memory roadmap, but it adds an important security capability while preserving compatibility with existing workflows.

10. Install RagLeap Memory 0.3.1

Standard installation:

pip install ragleap-memory==0.3.1

With encrypted export/import support:

pip install "ragleap-memory[crypto]==0.3.1"

Project resources:

  • GitHub: https://github.com/ragleap/ragleap-core
  • PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/ragleap-memory/
  • Documentation: https://docs.ragleap.com/

Contributions, testing, security feedback, and technical discussions are welcome through the official repository.

Final thoughts

AI memory is becoming a foundational part of intelligent systems.

As AI employees take on more responsibilities, their memory infrastructure needs to be reliable, controlled, portable, and designed with security boundaries in mind.

With RagLeap Memory 0.3.1, we have added encrypted memory export and import, context binding, tamper detection, and extensive release verification.

We will continue developing RagLeap's memory infrastructure with a focus on security, reliability, and self-hosted control.

RagLeap — Open-source AI employees that ask before they act.
