title: Python While Loop: Display Odd and Even Jersey Numbers
summary:
In a school sports event, students wearing ODD jersey numbers enter the ground first. After they finish, students wearing EVEN jersey numbers enter the ground.

Let's use Python to display the order.

Displaying Odd Jersey Numbers

odd_no=1
print(odd_no,end=" ")
odd_no=odd_no+2
print(odd_no,end=" ")
odd_no=odd_no+2
print(odd_no,end=" ")
odd_no=odd_no+2
print(odd_no,end=" ")
odd_no=odd_no+2
print(odd_no,end=" ")
odd_no=odd_no+2

odd_no=1
while odd_no<=10:
print(odd_no,end=" ")
odd_no=odd_no+2

output 1 3 5 7 9

even_no=2
print(even_no,end=" ")
even_no=even_no+2
print(even_no,end=" ")
even_no=even_no+2
print(even_no,end=" ")
even_no=even_no+2
print(even_no,end=" ")
even_no=even_no+2
print(even_no,end=" ")
even_no=even_no+2

even_no=2
while even_no<=10:
print(even_no,end=" ")
even_no=even_no+2

output 2 4 6 8 10

combined program
print("Odd Jersey Numbers:")

odd_no=1
while odd_no<=10:
print(odd_no,end=" ")
odd_no=odd_no+2

print("\nEven Jersey Number:")

eeven_no=2
while even_no<=10:
print(even_no,end=" ")
even_no=even_no+2

Output:

Odd Jersey Numbers:
1 3 5 7 9

Even Jersey Number:
2 4 6 8 10

title: 為什麼 osFoundry 讓 Codex CLI 針對每個資源輪詢 cursor，而不是主動推送變更？
summary:
想知道「什麼東西變了」的 client，osFoundry 的 MCP server 能給的就只有下面這些。在這台 Mac 上、不帶 token 執行：

$ uv run --with tiktoken --with jsonschema python3 watch_sim.py
== Part 1: live wire, 8 calls each, ms ==
initialize                   HTTP 200  median  414.7  p90  757.8
tools/list                   HTTP 200  median  606.8  p90  716.7
resources/subscribe          HTTP 200  median  450.6  p90  550.2
GET (stream)                 HTTP 405  median  423.9  p90  475.4
tools/call poll (no token)   HTTP 401  median  322.0  p90  463.9
initialize capabilities: {"tools": {"listChanged": false}}
resources/subscribe -> {"code": -32601, "message": "Method not found"}
GET body -> ''
poll without token -> isError True | Authentication required
rate limit headers: limit 2000, reset in 61 s

三條 push 的路都關著。initialize 只宣告了 tools，其他什麼都沒有，而且是 listChanged: false，所以連 tool 清單變動都不會通知。resources/subscribe 回的是 "Method not found"。對 MCP URL 發 GET，也就是 Streamable HTTP server 原本會開出 server 到 client 串流的地方，回傳 405。剩下的只有一個唯讀 tool：

{"name": "poll_resource_events",
 "description": "Resume from an event sequence for one granted channel, Note, knowledge base, record, or session.",
 "inputSchema": {"properties": {
     "resource_type": {"enum": ["message_channel", "note", "knowledge_base", "record_channel", "room",
                                "gitnest_repository", "agent_session", "team_session", "loop_session",
                                "graph_session"]},
     "resource_id": {"type": "string"},
     "after_sequence": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 0},
     "limit": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 100}},
   "required": ["resource_type", "resource_id"], "additionalProperties": false},
 "annotations": {"readOnlyHint": true, "openWorldHint": false, "destructiveHint": false},
 "securitySchemes": [{"type": "oauth2", "scopes": ["osfoundry:read"]}]}

"One granted" 的資源、"resume from an event sequence"。這篇接下來就是在講這幾個字，client 端則用 Python 重建。這台機器沒有安裝 codex 執行檔，所以由 script 扮演 client。osFoundry 的 server 程式碼沒有公開：Part 1 和 Part 2 打的是正式環境的 server，Part 3 則是重建版本，回應格式和活動頻率都是它自己設定的。

為什麼 Codex 特別適合用輪詢，而不是 push？

Codex CLI 不是 daemon。你執行它，它才會跑，做完一個 turn 之後就結束，或是停下來等你。Push channel 需要有東西在你的 session 之間持續監聽，而在筆電上，這個東西往往不存在。Sequence cursor 剛好符合這種使用方式：client 每個資源只記一個整數，想回來的時候再回來，問「這個號碼之後發生了什麼」。

上面的毫秒數是在日本用 Apple M1 量的，所以反映的多半是網路路徑，而不是 server 本身。更重要的是 rate limit header。未驗證的回應帶有 X-RateLimit-Limit: 2000，大約 61 s 後重置。登入後的 client 是否有同樣的額度沒有另外確認，但就算每 30 s 輪詢 30 個資源，也才每分鐘 60 個請求。限制 Codex 監看程式的不是 server 負載，而是它自己的 turn：每一次 poll 都是一次 tool call，模型得發出去、再讀回來。

Client 怎麼知道自己可以輪詢哪些資源？

靠兩個呼叫，而 schema 本身就透露了不少設計思路：

list_granted_resources   osfoundry:read  ro=True required=[] props=[]
list_project_resources   osfoundry:read  ro=True required=['project_id', 'resource_type'] props=['project_id', 'resource_type', 'search', 'offset', 'limit']
poll_resource_events     osfoundry:read  ro=True required=['resource_type', 'resource_id'] props=['resource_type', 'resource_id', 'after_sequence', 'limit']
59 tools on server; these three = 591 of 12662 tokens (4.7%, cl100k_base)
poll_resource_events types: 10 | list_project_resources types: 9 | only pollable: ['graph_session']

list_granted_resources 完全不接受參數，schema 也把加參數的路堵死了：

list_granted_resources   no arguments           ok
list_granted_resources   project_id passed      REJECT additionalProperties

這是 server 告訴 client 它擁有什麼，而不是 client 去要求什麼。initialize 的 instructions 第一句就是 "Use list_granted_resources first." 回傳的內容是加到這個連線的 project，以及個別授權的資源。在 web client（ExternalAssistantsPanel.tsx）裡，對應的是 Projects 區塊和 "Older individual access"。

list_project_resources 一定要帶 resource_type。沒有「列出這個 project 裡所有東西」的方式，所以要盤點完整內容，每種類型就要呼叫一次，總共九種；某個類型超過 50 筆的話還要更多次（limit 上限 50，用 offset 分頁）。它的 description 還補充了 project 存取的唯一例外："Ordinary Message channels require a separate invitation."

graph_session 可以輪詢，但不能列出。Graph 存在 owner 的桌面上，要透過 list_graph_sessions 進來，而且前提是 owner 已經從桌面 app 分享出來。

為什麼 cursor 由 client 持有，而不是 server？

osFoundry 兩種都有。Agent network 上的 wait_for_messages 會幫你記住 cursor："Without after_sequence it resumes where your last call stopped"，而且支援 timeout_s 最多 50 的 long polling。poll_resource_events 兩者都沒有。timeout_s 會被拒絕，description 也只寫 "resume from"，所以號碼要由 client 自己帶：

wait_for_messages props: ['after_sequence', 'timeout_s', 'limit'] timeout_s max 50 | poll_resource_events has timeout: False
poll_resource_events     timeout_s 30           REJECT additionalProperties

Server 端持有 cursor，對單一監聽者來說很方便。但只要兩個 client 共用同一個連線就會出問題，而你用同一個登入在兩個終端機開 Codex 時，正好就是這種情況。重建版本讓 600 個 channel 事件經過兩個隨機輪流輪詢的終端機：

two terminals, client cursor: A saw 600/600, B saw 600/600
two terminals, server cursor: A saw 305/600, B saw 295/600

每個連線一個 server 端 cursor 的話，每個終端機都會替另一個把 cursor 往前推，結果各自只看到大約一半。Request 裡帶 after_sequence 的話，兩邊都能看到全部，server 也完全不需要保存每個讀取者的狀態。對於可能被多個工具各自讀取的資源 log 來說，cursor 交給 client 才是對的。

Schema 沒有把 after_sequence 設為必填，也沒說省略時代表什麼。不要依賴這個行為。把號碼存下來，每次都帶上。

一整頁要花多少次呼叫？

limit 最多 100。大量匯入之後，一則 note 可能有好幾百個事件在等。要清空，就得從最後一個 sequence 繼續呼叫，直到回來的頁面不滿為止：

burst of 350 events, limit 100:  4 calls to drain, cursor ends at 350
burst of 350 events, limit  50:  7 calls to drain, cursor ends at 350

resources/subscribe -> {"code": -32601, "message": "Method not found"}

Codex CLI 不是 daemon。你執行它，它才會跑，做完一個 turn 之後就結束，或是停下來等你。Push channel 需要有東西在你的 session 之間持續監聽，而在筆電上，這個東西往往不存在。Sequence cursor 剛好符合這種使用方式：client 每個資源只記一個整數，想回來的時候再回來，問「這個號碼之後發生了什麼」。

title: A practical portrait review workflow and crop-boundary check
summary:
A profile photo has a small job: help another person recognize you and get a sense of how you present yourself. That can be harder than it sounds. A picture that looks appealing at full size may be unreadable on a phone, while a technically sharp image may feel too formal for the setting. Instead of searching for one perfect portrait, build a small set of honest, varied images and review them together.

AI Dating Photo Generator is a browser-based tool that creates dating profile portraits from your own photos, lets you choose a scene, and offers a way to review or refine results. If you decide to explore the ai dating profile photo generator, treat generated images as options to evaluate rather than as proof of what you look like in every situation. I am associated with the project, and this guide was drafted with AI assistance. Examples are hypothetical, and it does not claim independent product testing or guaranteed results.

Start with recognition, not decoration

Before changing a background or choosing an outfit, decide what a viewer should be able to recognize. A clear view of your face, an expression that feels natural, and a recent appearance are more important than a dramatic location. A useful first image should still make sense at the small size at which most people will encounter it.

Compare a candidate with a recent, unedited photograph. Check features that matter for recognition, including the shape of your face, hairstyle, facial hair, and any distinctive marks you normally show. Lighting and a different camera angle can change how someone looks, but a generated image should not make a meeting in person feel like a surprise. If you would need to explain that the picture represents an old hairstyle or a substantially different appearance, choose a more current alternative.

Gather a useful source set

When selecting input images, use photographs you have permission to upload and share. Prefer images of yourself over pictures containing other people. A varied source set can include a straight-on portrait, a gentle three-quarter angle, and a picture in even daylight. Avoid relying entirely on images with heavy filters, deep shadows, face coverings, or very low resolution.

More files are not automatically better. Review each photo for focus, current appearance, and whether your face is large enough to distinguish. Set aside any image whose ownership or consent is uncertain. If a group photograph is your only option, consider taking a fresh individual picture instead of uploading other people’s faces unnecessarily.

Keep the original files in a private location. Before using any external service, read its current terms and privacy information, including what it says about uploads, retention, deletion, and permitted uses. Do not assume that a file disappears immediately after you close a browser tab. If the available information does not meet your comfort level, use an offline photo or another method instead.

Choose a setting that supports the subject

A background should add context without competing with your face. A simple outdoor scene, an uncluttered room, or a neutral wall can be easier to read than a busy street full of signs and strangers. Think about the mood you want to convey: relaxed, approachable, creative, or active. A setting can suggest a mood without making a factual claim about your occupation or lifestyle.

Review the boundaries where hair, clothing, and shoulders meet the background. Generated portraits may contain odd edges, inconsistent shadows, or details that look plausible at a glance but not on inspection. Look at hands, jewelry, glasses, fabric patterns, and objects close to the body. If a feature looks wrong, refine or discard the image rather than hoping nobody notices.

A convincing scene is not necessarily an accurate one. Avoid selecting a location that implies you visited a place or participated in an activity if you did not. A neutral illustrative setting is easier to interpret honestly than a picture that appears to document a specific trip or event. When in doubt, pair a generated portrait with real, recent photographs that show your everyday appearance.

Check light, color, and framing

Good lighting reveals the face without flattening every detail. Look for a balance between visible eyes, natural skin tones, and enough contrast to separate the subject from the background. Very bright highlights can erase detail, while strong backlighting can turn a face into a silhouette. Color should feel consistent across the image; a warm face against an implausibly cool shadow may be distracting.

Test the crop before deciding. Leave some space around the head and shoulders so the image can survive different app layouts. A square preview may crop differently from a tall profile card. Keep important facial features away from the extreme edges, and verify that hair or the top of the head is not unintentionally cut off.

Look at the image on both a larger display and a phone. At a large size, inspect artifacts. At a small size, ask whether the expression is readable and whether the subject stands out from the background. A photo can pass one test and fail the other. Keep only images that work in the context in which they will be seen.

Build variety across a set

A profile usually benefits from more than several nearly identical close-ups. Consider a clear primary portrait, a different angle or setting, and a candid or activity image that reflects something you actually enjoy. Each picture should contribute information rather than repeat the same expression in a slightly different crop.

Variety does not mean presenting incompatible versions of yourself. A collection that switches dramatically between ages, hair colors, body shapes, or styles can undermine recognition. title: Normalizing U.S. Company Names Before You Match Them
summary:
Company names from different sources rarely agree character for character. "The Acme Group, L.L.C.", "ACME GROUP LLC" and "Acme Group" could be one entity or three. A normalized name gives you a stable comparison key, as long as you remember what the key discards.

What usually needs cleaning

Case and spacing. Pick one case, trim the ends, and collapse repeated spaces.

Punctuation. Periods, commas, and quotes are noise. Curly and straight apostrophes should end up identical, or be removed. An ampersand is safest as the word "and."

Accents. "Peña" and "Pena" should compare equal. Unicode normalization followed by an ASCII fold handles the common cases.

Legal endings. LLC and L.L.C., Inc. and Incorporated, Corp. and Corporation, Co. and Company, Ltd. and Limited, plus LP, LLP, and PLLC. Map the spellings to one short form and move it out of the name into a field of its own. It tells you the entity type, and "Acme Inc" and "Acme LLC" can be two separate legal entities.

A leading "The". Sources disagree on whether to keep it, so the key should not depend on it.

Trade names. A string like "Acme Group LLC dba Bright Path" holds two names. Split on dba, d/b/a, aka, or fka and keep both parts, labeled. Matching on the trade name alone can attach a record to the wrong legal entity.

Same name, different state

Identical names across states are common, because each state checks name availability only against its own registry. A key that ignores the state will merge strangers. Put the state, or the registry the record came from, into the key, and treat a cross-state match as a lead to confirm with other fields.

A teaching example

This is a teaching example, not production code. It returns the state, the core name, the entity-type ending, and any trade name found after dba, aka, or fka.

import re
import unicodedata
ENDINGS = {"INCORPORATED": "INC", "CORPORATION": "CORP", "COMPANY": "CO", "LIMITED": "LTD"}
ENDINGS.update({e: e for e in ("LLC", "INC", "CORP", "CO", "LTD", "LP", "LLP", "PLLC")})
ALIAS = re.compile(r"\b(?:D[./]?B[./]?A|A[./]?K[./]?A|F[./]?K[./]?A)\b\.?", re.I)

def words(text):
    text = unicodedata.normalize("NFKD", text).encode("ascii", "ignore").decode()
    text = text.upper().replace("&", " AND ").replace(".", "").replace("'", "")
    return re.findall(r"[A-Z0-9]+", text)

def company_key(raw, state):
    legal, *alias = ALIAS.split(raw, maxsplit=1)
    core = words(legal)
    ending = ENDINGS.get(core[-1], "") if core else ""
    while core and core[-1] in ENDINGS:
        core.pop()
    core = core[1:] if core[:1] == ["THE"] else core
    return state.upper(), " ".join(core), ending, " ".join(words("".join(alias)))

Two calls show the behavior, including an edge case:

company_key("The Acme Group, L.L.C. d/b/a Bright Path", "tx")
# ('TX', 'ACME GROUP', 'LLC', 'BRIGHT PATH')
company_key("Peña & Co.", "or")
# ('OR', 'PENA AND', 'CO', '')

The second result leaves a dangling AND, because "& Co." is really part of how that firm writes its name. Rules like these are blunt, and every ruleset produces cases like this one.

Order matters as well. Split off the trade name before removing punctuation, or "d/b/a" falls apart into loose letters that look like part of the name.

To keep the rules honest, build a small table of pairs you know are the same entity and pairs you know are not, and rerun it whenever you change a rule. A fix for one case often breaks another.

What the key throws away

Normalization is lossy on purpose. Store the raw name next to the key, keep the ending and the trade name as separate fields, and never treat an equal key as proof of identity. Confirm with something the name cannot fake: a registry ID, a formation date, or a principal address.

title: Turn PDFs into Clean Markdown for ChatGPT and RAG (Without Uploading Them)
summary:
If you've ever pasted a PDF into ChatGPT or Claude and got an answer about the wrong section, the model probably wasn't the problem. The text was.

A PDF doesn't store "a heading", "a table" or "a paragraph". It stores pieces of text placed at positions on a page. When you copy that text out, you get whatever order the PDF happens to keep it in, and the structure is gone. For an LLM, and even more for a RAG pipeline, structure is half the information.

This post covers what goes wrong, what clean Markdown for AI should look like, and a short Python chunker that splits it for retrieval while keeping page numbers.

Disclosure: I built QuickCatPDF, the free converter I use in the examples. The format and the chunking code work with any converter that produces similar Markdown.

What breaks when you copy text out of a PDF

Copy and paste from a typical report and you'll usually see some of these:

  • Lines broken mid-sentence, because every visual line ends with a newline.
  • Two columns mixed together, line by line.
  • The page header and footer repeated on every page ("Annual Review 2026 · Page 7").
  • Tables flattened into a run of numbers with no idea which value belongs to which column.
  • Words split by hyphens at line ends ("docu- ment").
  • Links gone. In a PDF, a link's address isn't part of the text at all. It's stored separately as an annotation on top of the page, so plain copy-paste only gives you the visible words.

None of this stops a model from reading the text, but it makes it worse at finding the right part and at quoting numbers from tables correctly.

What "clean Markdown for an LLM" looks like

Markdown is a good middle ground: models read it naturally, it's compact, and it keeps the structure that matters.

---

source: "annual-review.pdf"
pages: 4
---



# Annual Review 2026

## Introduction

Revenue grew in every quarter...

## Results by quarter

| Quarter | Revenue | Growth |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | 1.2M | 4% |
| Q2 | 1.4M | 17% |

A few details are worth copying, whatever tool you use:

  1. Front matter naming the source file and page count. When you paste several documents into one chat, the model knows which is which.
  2. Page markers as HTML comments (). Models read them, rendered Markdown hides them, and your RAG answers can cite a page.
  3. Real headings (#, ##, ###) instead of bold lines.
  4. Pipe tables, so every value stays in its row and column.
  5. No page furniture: page numbers and repeated headers and footers removed, hyphenated words joined, wrapped lines merged into single paragraphs.

Three questions people keep asking

"How do I keep headings when converting PDF to Markdown?"
Most converters detect headings from the text's size and weight. That works when the PDF's headings are visibly larger or bold. If a document's headings are the same size and weight as the body text, there's no signal to detect, and they come out as plain paragraphs. In that case, add the ## markers by hand for the main sections. It takes a minute and makes a big difference for chunking.

"How do I keep tables?"
Pick a converter that outputs pipe tables, then check one table against the original. Tables without lines (columns separated only by white space, like bank statements) are the hardest case for any tool.

"Why are my hyperlinks lost?"
Because of the annotation point above: the address isn't in the text layer. A converter has to read the link annotations and match them to the words underneath. Plain copy-paste and many text extractors skip that step.

Chunking for RAG without losing page numbers

Headings are natural chunk boundaries, and the page comments let every chunk carry the page it started on. Here's a small, dependency-free chunker:

import re

def chunk_markdown(md: str, max_chars: int = 4000):
    """Split Markdown on ## headings, keeping the page number each chunk starts on."""
    md = re.sub(r"\A---\n.*?\n---\n", "", md, flags=re.S)  # drop front matter
    page = 1
    chunks, current, heading = [], [], None

    def flush():
        text = "\n".join(current).strip()
        if text:
            chunks.append({"heading": heading, "page": start_page, "text": text})

    start_page = page
    for line in md.splitlines():
        m = re.match(r"", line)
        if m:
            page = int(m.group(1))
            if not "".join(current).strip():
                start_page = page
            continue
        if line.startswith("## ") or sum(len(l) for l in current) > max_chars:
            flush()
            current, start_page = [], page
            if line.startswith("## "):
                heading = line[3:].strip()
        current.append(line)
    flush()
    return chunks

Each chunk comes back as {"heading": "Results by quarter", "page": 1, "text": "..."}, ready to embed. Store heading and page as metadata, and your answers can say "see page 1, Results by quarter" instead of pointing at the whole document.

If you prefer page-sized chunks (useful for contracts and forms), split on the comments instead.

Watch your token budget

A rough rule for English is about 4 characters per token, fewer for other scripts. That's close enough to decide whether a document fits in one prompt or needs chunking. Treat it as an estimate, not an exact count.

Doing it without uploading the PDF

Many PDFs you'd want to ask an AI about are exactly the ones you shouldn't hand to random websites: contracts, financial reports, internal docs. You'll decide later where the text goes. The conversion step doesn't need to send it anywhere.

The converter I built, QuickCatPDF's PDF to Markdown for LLMs, runs in the browser:

  1. Drop in up to 20 PDFs.
  2. Keep Front matter and Page markers as comments ticked.
  3. Optionally limit the Pages.
  4. Click Convert to Markdown, then copy or download. It shows the character count and a token estimate.

In my test, a 4-page report converted in about half a second into 4.6 KB of Markdown. Scanned PDFs are read with OCR in the browser too. You can check that nothing is uploaded: load the page, turn on airplane mode, and convert.

For plain Markdown for GitHub, Obsidian or Notion (with bold, italics, links and optional images), there's a separate PDF to Markdown tool.

Quick checklist

  • Don't paste raw PDF text into an LLM when structure matters. Convert to Markdown first.
  • Keep front matter and page markers, and drop the headers and footers.
  • Check one heading and one table against the original.
  • Chunk on ## headings and keep the page number as metadata.
  • Estimate tokens at about 4 characters per token for English.

What's the worst PDF you've had to feed into an LLM? Tables, multi-column layouts, scans? I'm collecting hard cases.

  1. Front matter naming the source file and page count. When you paste several documents into one chat, the model knows which is which.
  2. Page markers as HTML comments (). Models read them, rendered Markdown hides them, and your RAG answers can cite a page.
  3. Real headings (#, ##, ###) instead of bold lines.
  4. Pipe tables, so every value stays in its row and column.
  5. No page furniture: page numbers and repeated headers and footers removed, hyphenated words joined, wrapped lines merged into single paragraphs.

Three questions people keep asking

"How do I keep headings when converting PDF to Markdown?"
Most converters detect headings from the text's size and weight. That works when the PDF's headings are visibly larger or bold. If a document's headings are the same size and weight as the body text, there's no signal to detect, and they come out as plain paragraphs. In that case, add the ## markers by hand for the main sections. It takes a minute and makes a big difference for chunking.

"How do I keep tables?"
Pick a converter that outputs pipe tables, then check one table against the original. Tables without lines (columns separated only by white space, like bank statements) are the hardest case for any tool.

"Why are my hyperlinks lost?"
Because of the annotation point above: the address isn't in the text layer. A converter has to read the link annotations and match them to the words underneath. Plain copy-paste and many text extractors skip that step.

Chunking for RAG without losing page numbers

Headings are natural chunk boundaries, and the page comments let every chunk carry the page it started on. Here's a small, dependency-free chunker:

import re

def chunk_markdown(md: str, max_chars: int = 4000):
    """Split Markdown on ## headings, keeping the page number each chunk starts on."""
    md = re.sub(r"\A---\n.*?\n---\n", "", md, flags=re.S)  # drop front matter
    page = 1
    chunks, current, heading = [], [], None

    def flush():
        text = "\n".join(current).strip()
        if text:
            chunks.append({"heading": heading, "page": start_page, "text": text})

    start_page = page
    for line in md.splitlines():
        m = re.match(r"", line)
        if m:
            page = int(m.group(1))
            if not "".join(current).strip():
                start_page = page
            continue
        if line.startswith("## ") or sum(len(l) for l in current) > max_chars:
            flush()
            current, start_page = [], page
            if line.startswith("## "):
                heading = line[3:].strip()
        current.append(line)
    flush()
    return chunks

Each chunk comes back as {"heading": "Results by quarter", "page": 1, "text": "..."}, ready to embed. Store heading and page as metadata, and your answers can say "see page 1, Results by quarter" instead of pointing at the whole document.

If you prefer page-sized chunks (useful for contracts and forms), split on the comments instead.

Watch your token budget

A rough rule for English is about 4 characters per token, fewer for other scripts. That's close enough to decide whether a document fits in one prompt or needs chunking. Treat it as an estimate, not an exact count.

Quick checklist

  • Don't paste raw PDF text into an LLM when structure matters. Convert to Markdown first.
  • Keep front matter and page markers, and drop the headers and footers.
  • Check one heading and one table against the original.
  • Chunk on ## headings and keep the page number as metadata.
  • Estimate tokens at about 4 characters per token for English.
